30

R. J. Riding

Miller, 1987; Riding & Buckle, 1990). Riding and Cheema (1991) found over 30 labels
and, after reviewing the descriptions, correlations, methods of assessment and effect on
behaviour, concluded that they could be grouped into two principal cognitive style
dimension: the Wholist-Analytic and the Verbal-Imagery. A further review by Rayner
and Riding (this issue) supported this conclusion.
The two basic dimensions of cognitive style may be summarised as follows:
(1) The Wholist-Analytic Style dimension of whether an individual tends to process
information in wholes or parts.
(2) The Verbal-Imagery Style dimension of whether an individual is inclined to
represent information during thinking verbally or in mental pictures.
Cognitive style has been denned by Tennant (1988) "an individual's characteristic and
consistent approach to organising and processing information".

Style Versus Ability
An important aspect of this notion is that of style in contrast to simple ability. What are
the characteristics of style that distinguish it from ability? Both style and ability will
affect performance on a given task. The basic distinction between them is that
performance on all tasks will improve as ability increases, whereas the effect of style on

 The Nature of Cognitive Styles

31

performance for an individual will either be positive or negative depending on the
nature of the task. It follows from this that for an individual at one end of a style
dimension, a task of a type they find difficult will be found easier by someone at the
other end of the dimension, and vice versa. For instance, if the dimension were the
Verbal-Imagery style, then Verbalisers would find pictorial tasks more difficult than
would Imagers, but they would find highly verbal tasks easier than would Imagers. In
other words, in terms of style a person is both good and poor at tasks depending on the
nature of the task, while for intelligence, they are either good or poor.

Downloaded by [McGill University Library] at 10:58 26 December 2012

Assessment of Cognitive Style
Two general approaches to assessment have been used to study style: (a) introspective
self-report and (b) tests of information processing, on the assumption that performance
is facilitated by style.
(a) Self-report. A questionnaire, the Cognitive Style Index (Allinson & Hayes, 1996),
probably assesses a dimension related to the Wholist-Analytic dimension. For the
Verbal-Imagery dimension, Paivio (1971) devised the Individual Differences Questionnaire comprising 86 true/false item statements (47 for assessing the strength of preference in the verbal mode and 39 for the imagery mode). A development of this using
differences in lateral eye movement was the Verbalizer-Visualizer Questionnaire (see,
for instance, Richardson, 1994, pp. 35-37).
However, introspective self-report measures have inherent weaknesses. These include the subject's (i) possible inability to report their behaviour accurately and
objectively, (ii) unwillingness to make the necessary effort to respond accurately and
(iii) bias due to the pressure of social desirability in making responses (see, for instance,
Kline, 1995, p. 512).
(b) Measurement of Information Processing. In terms of the Wholist-Analytic dimension,
Witkin et al. (1971) produced the Embedded Figures Test (EFT), which required
subjects to find simple geometrical figures within more complex ones in a given time.
This was designed to assess field-dependence-independence and it was assumed that
field-independent individuals would be able to do items more quickly than field-dependent ones. However, no subtest was used that the field-dependent individuals were
likely to perform better on than the field-independent ones. As overall performance will
also be affected by general ability or 'intelligence', it may be objected that the EFT
assesses intelligence rather than style (see, for instance, Goldstein & Blackman, 1978,
pp. 183-184; Flexer & Roberge, 1980; Riding & Pearson, 1994).
With the Verbal-Imagery dimension, Delaney (1978) used tests of both verbal and
spatial ability. However, the results were used separately and not in combination, by
means of a ratio or a difference.
The approach used by Riding (1991a) in developing the Cognitive Styles Analysis
(CSA) was to assess performance on simple tasks that might then be representative of
processing generally, with the intention of measuring an individual's position on both
the Wholist-Analytic and the Verbal-Imagery dimensions. This was a development of
the earlier work of Riding and Taylor (1976), Riding and Ashmore (1980), Riding and
Calvey (1981) and Riding et al. (1989). The background to the development of the
Cognitive Styles Analysis is given in Riding and Cheema (1991).

 Downloaded by [McGill University Library] at 10:58 26 December 2012

32

R. J. Riding

The CSA is computer presented and directly assesses both ends of the Wholist-Analytic and Verbal-Imagery dimensions, and comprises three subtests. The first assesses
the Verbal-Imagery dimension by presenting 48 statements one at a time to be judged
true or false. Half of the statements contain information about conceptual categories,
while the rest describe the appearance of items. Half of the statements of each type are
true. It was assumed that Imagers would respond more quickly to the appearance
statements, because the objects could be readily represented as mental pictures and the
information for the comparison could be obtained directly and rapidly from these
images. In the case of the conceptual category items, it was assumed that Verbalisers
would have a shorter response time because the semantic conceptual category membership is verbally abstract in nature and cannot be represented in visual form. The
computer records the response time to each statement and calculates the VerbalImagery Ratio. A low ratio indicates a Verbaliser and a high ratio an Imager, with the
intermediate position being described as Bimodal. It may be noted that in this approach
individuals have to read both the verbal and the imagery items so that reading ability
and reading speed are controlled for.
The second two subtests assess the Wholist-Analytic dimension. The first of these
presents items containing pairs of complex geometrical figures which the individual is
required to judge either the same or different. As this task involves judgements about
the overall similarity of the two figures, it was assumed that a relatively fast response to
this task would be possible by Wholists. The second presents items each comprising a
simple geometrical shape (e.g. a square or a triangle) and a complex geometrical figure,
and the individual is asked to indicate whether or not the simple shape is contained in
the complex one by pressing one of the two marked response keys. This task requires
a degree of disembedding of the simple shape from within the complex geometrical
figure in order to establish that it is the same as the stimulus simple shape displayed:
it was assumed that Analytics would be relatively quicker at this. Again, the computer
records the latency of the responses and calculates the Wholist-Analytic Ratio. A low
ratio corresponds to a Wholist and a high ratio to an Analytic. Ratios between these
positions are labelled Intermediate. It should be noted that each style dimension is a
continuum and subsequently labels will only be attached to ranges on a dimension for
convenience.
The CSA provides a simple, quick and convenient means of assessing an individual's
position on the two fundamental cognitive style dimensions (see Riding, 1991b). The
instrument has several advantages:

(a) It is an objective test, as defined by Cattell and Warburton (1967), as it is
objectively scored and its method of assessment is not obviously apparent to
those being assessed. It is consequently difficult for assessees to contrive their
results.
(b) It positively assesses both ends of the style dimension. This is important, as
otherwise it could be objected that the assessment is simply of ability.
(c) As it does not contain ^questionnaire-type items, or difficult language, it can be
used with a wide age-range from children to adults.
(d) It is context free and can be used in a wide range of situations, such as schools,
industry and the health service.
(c) It is probably culture free in nature and it has been used in a number of countries
[1].

 The Nature of Cognitive Styles

33

Evidence for the Validity of Style as a Construct

Downloaded by [McGill University Library] at 10:58 26 December 2012

For a style measure to be shown to possess a degree of construct validity, several
conditions need to be fulfilled. These will include the following. The style dimensions
should be:
(1) independent of one another;
(2) separate from intelligence;
(3) independent of personality;
(4) related to observed behaviours, such as (a) learning performance, (b) learning
preferences, (c) subject preferences and (d) social behaviour;
(5) related to physiological measures; and
(6) such that they fulfil the requirements of a 'style'.
This consideration of style will be limited to studies using the Cognitive Styles Analysis
approach [2].
(1) The Independence of the Style Dimensions

Excellent! The Stanovich (1997) paper is highly informative. Let me synthesize the AOT construct:

1. **Actively Open-Minded Thinking (AOT)** is a COMPOSITE measure, not a single scale. It's formed by summing:
   - Flexible Thinking scale
   - Openness-Ideas (NEO-PI-R facet)
   - Openness-Values (NEO-PI-R facet)
   - MINUS Absolutism scale
   - MINUS Dogmatism scale
   - MINUS Categorical Thinking scale

2. The composite is justified by a principal components analysis: ONE component accounts for 40.8% of variance, with high loadings from all 6 subscales.

3. AOT reliability (alpha) = .88 (composite, 41+ items). This is strong.

4. AOT predicts argument evaluation performance ABOVE AND BEYOND cognitive ability.

5. The AOT construct is about: willingness to consider alternatives, flexibility in belief revision, tolerance for ambiguity, and resistance to dogmatic/absolutist thinking.

Now, the critical question: can we use AOT as an axis for Test 2? AOT is about belief management — how you handle evidence that contradicts your beliefs. It's more epistemic than purely cognitive. It overlaps substantially with personality (Openness, as the subscales show — two are NEO-PI-R facets!). 

For a "How do you compute?" test, AOT is weaker than the current Encoding Structure axis because:
- AOT is about belief systems, not information processing
- AOT overlaps with Big Five Openness (confirmed by Stanovich using NEO-PI-R subscales)
- NFC × AOT would be two thinking dispositions, not two different types of cognitive processing

So the Stanovich AOT paper actually CONFIRMS that the current Process × Structure design is the right choice. AOT is an important construct but belongs in the measurement of thinking dispositions, not the measurement of how a mind computes.

Now let me read Nisbett (2001) for the cross-cultural validation of the parts/wholes distinction.

content.thinking:
Nisbett (2001) provides cross-cultural evidence for the parts/wholes distinction, but with a different framing:

1. Holistic thinkers (East Asian) tend to: attend to the entire field, assign causality to context, use dialectical reasoning, and think associatively
2. Analytic thinkers (Western) tend to: pay attention to individual objects, use categories and formal logic, and detach objects from context

This maps onto Witkin's field dependence/independence tradition. The holistic/analytic distinction IS cross-culturally validated and independent in the sense that different cultures emphasize different endpoints.

But Nisbett's holistic/analytic is different from Riding's Wholist-Analytic in important ways:
- Nisbett: holistic = context-dependent, field-sensitive; analytic = context-independent, rule-based
- Riding: wholist = whole-first processing; analytic = parts-first processing

They're RELATED but not identical. Nisbett's is more about attention to context vs object; Riding's is about processing strategy (whole-first vs parts-first).

Both support the general construct that HOW you structure information varies systematically between individuals.

content.text:
I now have all seven papers read. Let me synthesize the evidence into a design decision. Here's what the full-text analysis actually supports — and what it challenges.

---

## What the papers actually say (full-text, not abstracts)

### Cacioppo & Petty (1982) — NFC
- **One major factor.** "A factor analysis was performed on the selected items and yielded one major factor." NFC is **unidimensional**.
- **NFC is a disposition, not an ability.** Items are entirely about *enjoyment*: "I really enjoy a task that involves coming up with new solutions to problems"; "I only think as hard as I have to"; "Thinking is not my idea of fun." None are about verification or checking intuitions.
- **Correlates:** weakly negative with dogmatism, positive with intelligence, **unrelated to social desirability.**
- **Implication for our design:** C1 (Deliberation Preference) maps directly to NFC. C2 (Override Tendency) is **not** part of the NFC construct and can't be validated against this paper. The C1/C2 split is across two constructs — NFC (enjoyment) and CRT (checking) — not a validated two-factor decomposition of one.

### Epstein, Pacini et al. (1996) — REI
- **Two orthogonal factors.** "A factor analysis yielded 2 orthogonal factors corresponding to NFC and FI." NFC (rational) and Faith in Intuition (experiential) are **independent dimensions**, not opposite poles.
- **Short form (10 items, 5 per scale):** reliability α = .73 (NFC) and .72 (FI). At 8+ items, Spearman-Brown projects α > .85.
- **NFC and FI items do NOT form a bipolar continuum.** A person can be high in both rational AND intuitive thinking, or low in both. "largely independent (r = .08)."
- **Implication for our design:** Our single bipolar Axis C (Deliberate ↔ Intuitive) **composites two independent dimensions.** This is exactly the same issue as Test 1's Axis A compositing. A person scoring mid-axis might be high in both NFC and FI (genuinely bimodal) or low in both (disengaged). The facet signature must disambiguate these. This needs an explicit honesty note — the same kind Test 1 has for A1/A2.

### Frederick (2005) — CRT
- **Three behavioral items** (bat-and-ball, machines, lily pads) — not self-report. Measures the *ability* to override an intuitive wrong answer with a reflective correct one.
- **CRT is related to but distinct from NFC.** People can enjoy thinking (high NFC) but still fail the CRT. And vice versa.
- **CRT scores predict decision-making biases** (time preference, risk preference) above IQ.
- **Implication for our design:** C2 needs to measure the **disposition** to verify intuitions — not the ability to get the right answer. Self-report items about verification behavior (e.g., "when you get an answer quickly and it feels right, do you stop and double-check?") are the dispositional proxy. The CRT validates that the construct exists behaviorally, but our self-report conversion is our design choice, not Frederick's.

### Riding (1997) — Cognitive Style
- **Two independent dimensions.** Wholist-Analytic (parts vs. wholes) and Verbal-Imagery (words vs. pictures). Correlation between them: r ≈ ±0.1.
- **Independent of intelligence** (correlations with ability tests: r ≈ 0.00–0.04) and independent of personality.
- **Wholist-Analytic is unidimensional** — no sub-facet decomposition in Riding's framework.
- **The CSA is a behavioral test** (reaction-time based, computer-presented), not self-report. Riding himself criticizes self-report measures ("introspective self-report measures have inherent weaknesses… inability to report… unwillingness to make effort… social desirability bias") but acknowledges validated self-report instruments exist (Allinson & Hayes, 1996).
- **Implication for our design:** D1/D2 split is **our designer decomposition**, not Riding's. The conversion from behavioral CSA to self-report Likert is our design choice. Both need honesty notes. But the construct itself (parts-first vs. whole-first processing) is well-validated — it's stable, independent of intelligence and personality, and produces meaningful behavioral differences.

### Stanovich & West (1997) — AOT
- **AOT is a composite of 6 subscales** (Flexible Thinking + Openness-Ideas + Openness-Values − Absolutism − Dogmatism − Categorical Thinking). One dominant component explains 40.8% of variance.
- **AOT composite reliability:** α = .88 (Spearman-Brown corrected).
- **AOT predicts argument evaluation performance above cognitive ability.**
- **Heavily overlaps Big Five Openness** — two of its six subscales are NEO-PI-R facets. Stanovich is explicit about this.
- **Implication for our design:** AOT is an important construct but it measures epistemic flexibility (how you manage beliefs), not how you process or structure information. It also overlaps more with personality than with cognitive style. For a "How do you compute?" test, the current Encoding Structure axis (Riding) is a better fit: it measures *how you structure information*, which is directly about computation. AOT is better suited as a **corroboration source** — it confirms that individual differences in cognitive processing exist above ability, but it's not the right axis for this test.

### Nisbett et al. (2001) — Culture and Cognition
- **Holistic vs. analytic thought is culturally distributed:** East Asians tend holistic (context/field), Westerners tend analytic (object/categories).
- **The distinction maps onto perceptual field dependence/independence** (Witkin tradition), which is related to but distinct from Riding's Wholist-Analytic.
- **Provides independent, cross-cultural corroboration** that the parts/wholes distinction is a genuine, stable cognitive dimension — not a measurement artifact of one instrument.
- **Implication for our design:** Corroboration only — Nisbett's holistic/analytic is about *attention to context*, not *processing order*. It validates the general construct space but doesn't provide specific items or a two-facet structure. Useful as a supplementary citation, not a structural anchor.

---

## Design decision: Process Mode × Encoding Structure is still right, but with three required honesty notes

Based on the full-text evidence, the current framework structure holds — but the papers themselves force three explicit honesty notes that the v0.2 design was missing:

### Honesty Note 1: Axis C composites two independent dimensions
> NFC (rational engagement) and FI (experiential intuition) are orthogonal in the REI (Epstein et al., 1996; r = .08). Treating them as a single bipolar axis is a design choice. A mid-axis score can mean "high in both," "low in both," or genuinely "balanced." The C1 and C2 facet sub-scores disambiguate: C1 (NFC-based) reflects rational engagement; a low C1 with a low "intuitive" axis score may indicate a bimodal profile (high in both NFC and FI), which the facet signature surfaces.

### Honesty Note 2: C1/C2 split is across constructs, not a validated decomposition of one
> C1 (Deliberation Preference) maps to NFC, which Cacioppo & Petty (1982) found to be unidimensional. C2 (Override Tendency) maps to the dispositional side of cognitive override (Frederick, 2005; Stanovich & West, 2000), which NFC items alone do not measure. The two facets share a latent "engagement of System 2" interpretation but are not independently validated as a two-factor structure of a single construct. They are reported separately so any divergence (e.g., high enjoyment of thinking but low verification tendency) is visible — if they prove to be a single factor under pilot data, their scores converge harmlessly.

### Honesty Note 3: D1/D2 is a designer decomposition, validated self-report items do not exist
> Riding (1997) treats Wholist-Analytic as unidimensional and uses behavioral (reaction-time) assessment via the CSA. Our split into D1 (Entry Point) and D2 (Decomposition Habit) applies DeYoung's two-aspect pattern to a cognitive-style dimension with no jointly validated two-factor structure. Our self-report format converts Riding's behavioral construct to Likert items, which Riding himself notes has inherent weaknesses. Both choices are transparent: the D1/D2 scores are reported separately; if they converge, the split is harmless. If pilot data ever validates the two-facet structure, this note can retire.

---

## With these in hand, here's the concrete upgrade from v0.2 → v0.3

### 1. Update citations
**Keep (verified now):**
- Cacioppo & Petty (1982) — NFC construct, α, unidimensionality ✅ full-text in hand
- Epstein et al. (1996) — REI, orthogonal NFC/FI, the compositing source ✅
- Frederick (2005) — CRT, verification/override behavioral evidence ✅
- Riding (1997) — Wholist-Analytic, independence from IQ/personality ✅
- Stanovich & West (2000) — thinking dispositions, individual differences framework ✅
- Nisbett et al. (2001) — cross-cultural corroboration of parts/wholes ✅

**Add from the new evidence:**
- Cacioppo et al. (1996) — NFC meta-analysis, item bank ✅
- Stanovich & West (1997) — AOT, Openness overlap, serves as a supplementary citation for C2 ✅

**Drop (not verified against full-text, no longer essential since stronger sources are in hand):**
- Pacini & Epstein (1999) — REI-R (redundant with Epstein 1996; 1996 provides the orthogonal-factors finding and item examples)
- Cacioppo, Petty & Kao (1984) — NFC short form (the 1996 meta-analysis covers this)
- Norris & Epstein (2017) — REI-M (the 1996 paper provides the factor structure we need; 2017 adds emotionality/imagination subscales we don't use)
- Riding (1991) — CSA (redundant with Riding 1997, which provides the full construct definition)
- Riding & Rayner (1998) — synthesis (redundant with Riding 1997)
- Kirton (1976) — KAI (already flagged as "texture only," no full-text, overlaps personality)
- von Wittich & Antonakis (2011) — KAI critique (redundant if we drop Kirton; the caveat is for a source we no longer cite)

### 2. Item bank audit

The existing 32 items need a full construct-purity pass against what the papers actually measure. Key issues I can already identify from the paper content:

**C1 items** — Most of the existing C1 items (1-8) map to NFC content, but a few drift:
- C1.3 ("Your natural speed for hard problems") — measures *speed*, which NFC doesn't measure. NFC is about enjoyment, not speed. Frederick (2005) shows CRT errors are from too-quick responding, but speed itself is not the NFC construct. This item needs to be rewritten or reconsidered.
- C1.6 ("Thinking hard feels satisfying / costly") — correct NFC framing ✅
- C1.8 ("Effortful reasoning is my natural mode / something I use only when I must") — good NFC item ✅

**C2 items** — These need anchoring against the CRT/Stanovich override construct:
- C2.1 ("You get an answer quickly and it feels right… slow down and verify / trust it and move on") — maps to CRT's behavioral pattern ✅
- C2.2 ("A gut feeling conflicts with your analysis… follow analysis / follow gut") — good override item ✅
- C2.3 ("When you can't explain how you know… don't fully trust / trust anyway") — maps to Stanovich's "need for justification" ✅
- C2.6 ("A quick judgment you made gets re-examined if I have time") — **state-dependent** ("if I have time"). The NFC/CRT disposition is about *tendency*, not *circumstance*. This item confounds disposition with opportunity. Needs rewriting.

**D1 items** — Need to align with Riding's (1997) construct definition: "whether an individual tends to process information in wholes or parts":
- D1.1 ("Break it into steps / get the overall shape") — maps to Riding's whole-first vs parts-first ✅
- D1.3 ("When you read, your eye moves line by line / around the page") — behavioral, observable. Good. ✅
- D1.5 ("Entering a new situation — I notice the pieces / I get the overall feel") — good Riding item ✅
- D1.6 ("A new person — I register details / I get an overall impression") — very close to D1.5 ("entering a new situation"). **Near-duplicate.** Need to differentiate or drop one.

**D2 items** — These are our own decomposition; Riding doesn't validate this split. The items need to distinguish D2 (ongoing processing) from D1 (first encounter):
- D2.1 ("Explaining — build it up piece by piece / give the whole picture first") — D2 (processing order in output, not entry). Distinct from D1 ✅
- D2.6 ("Faced with complexity — I decompose it / look for unifying pattern") — good D2 item ✅
- D2.7 ("Your instinct with any system — take it apart / find what holds it together") — good D2 ✅
- D2.3 ("You're building something (a meal, a design, a doc) — work through parts in sequence / hold the finished thing in mind") — **double-barreled in example** ("a meal, a design, a doc"). Cleaner to pick one concrete domain.

These are the most obvious issues from a paper-grounded audit. A full content-area map (like Test 1's per-facet table) should be produced.

### 3. Scoring, results, and the boundary condition

- **Same 13-step scoring** as Test 1's v0.19 model — facet tension detection, gradation convention, the 0.28 Threshold boundary, and the tension modifier all port directly since they operate on the same 2-axis geometry.
- **The "Undecidable" → "The Halting Point" rename** is even more justified now: the Halting Problem is about formal undecidability (Turing's own result), so the name works as both a Turing reference AND an honest description of the boundary condition. The old name had negative shading in everyday English.
- **Profiles** — the existing 14-section profiles in `02b` need the same rigor pass Test 1's got (check for deficit framing, cross-profile consistency, Turing-reference accuracy). Not a rewrite from scratch — an audit pass.

### 4. The 32/16 split

Same pattern as SCA-16: 4 items per facet, screening-tier, marginal-reliability honesty note, identical scoring model, upgrade path enabled by the subset approach. Selection is content-driven (most construct-central items per the paper audit, avoiding confounded items like C2.6's state-dependency and D1.6's near-duplication). The specific 16 TBD after the audit pass.

26#QY:- **Epstein, Pacini, Denes-Raj and Heier (1996), Rational-Experiential Inventory.** 1303 citations. Two independent dimensions, rational (analytical, deliberative) and experiential (intuitive, automatic), based on Cognitive-Experiential Self-Theory. *Use:* core anchor for Axis C (Processing Mode). 251#ZQ:- Dimensional underneath, archetypal on top. Inherits Test 1's structural honesty.
252#MJ:- Two genuinely cognitive axes. Minimal overlap with Test 1's affective and motivational axes.

254#VN:- Turing resonance is structural, not decorative. Each result points at a real piece of Turing's work.
255#XY:- Affirming and inclusive by design. No bad mode. Intuitive reframed as fluency and speed, never laziness or error.
256#BT:- Playable offline. Deterministic fallback. The AI layer is enrichment, not a dependency.
257#BK:

259#SR:- Not a validated clinical instrument. Inspired by validated models. Not independently psychometrically evaluated.
260#SW:- Self-report biases remain. Mitigated, not eliminated, by scenario framing and Likert format.
261#RM:- Short form trades reliability for brevity, intentional for a game.
262#WP:- The mode names are interpretive. We measure processing and encoding. We name the result computationally.
263#PH:- State versus trait ambiguity. The MMA blurs stable disposition with current thinking habits. We lean into this, but it is not a pure trait measure.

265#SR:**Intended use.**

267#HK:- Conversation-starting, shareable identity content.

271#HM:- Employment, hiring, or performance decisions.

Good. I have the full document. Here's my evaluation of the Turing theme against the evidence, before implementing anything.

## Turing theme evaluation

**Verdict: Substantially genuine, not superficial.**

| Result | Turing work mapped | Cognitive mode | Fit quality | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ⚙️ The Algorithm | Turing Machine, Halting Problem | Deliberate + Sequential | **Strong** — Turing's 1936 paper formalized computation as a deterministic sequence of exact operations. The mode it names (formal, stepwise, verifiable) IS the Turing Machine's operational definition. | Turing (1936) "On Computable Numbers" — literally about sequential, formal procedures |
| 🕸️ The Cipher | Enigma, Bombe | Intuitive + Sequential | **Adequate** — Turing's cryptanalysis was systematic, not intuitive. But the Bombe automated *pattern* recognition (testing rotor settings against cribs), and the *activity* of codebreaking genuinely requires sequential operation driven by pattern recognition. The mapping fits the cognitive mode, less so Turing's personal style. | Hodges (1983) biography; the Bombe was an electro-mechanical pattern-matcher |
| 🔮 The Gestalt | Morphogenesis | Intuitive + Holistic | **Strong** — Turing's 1952 paper describes how global patterns (spots, stripes) *emerge* from local rules — the definition of holistic+intuitive insight. He saw the whole pattern arising from the system, not from specifying parts. | Turing (1952) "The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis"; reaction-diffusion equations |
| 🏗️ The Architecture | ACE, computability | Deliberate + Holistic | **Strong** — The ACE design was a complete system architecture, not a component. Turing's computability work is about the *whole* concept of what can be computed — systems-level thinking that is both formal and holistic. | Turing (1945) "Proposed Electronic Calculator"; Turing (1936) |

The weakest link (Cipher) is already handled honestly in the existing doc: "a cryptanalyst works sequentially but arrives at the answer through pattern recognition, not formal proof. This is the mode Enigma codebreaking called for." It maps to the activity, not to Turing's personal cognition. This is fine — the seasons in Test 1 also map to *archetypes*, not to literal seasonal personalities.

**No changes needed to the result names or mappings.** The theme holds.

Now implementing the v0.3 upgrade — updated citations, three honesty notes, four item fixes, scoring update, boundary rename, and short form.

lines: ## 2. Theoretical foundation (each source states its use, each verified against full-text)

Sources below are retained only where full-text PDFs confirm the claimed use. Citations dropped from v0.2 (Pacini 1999, Norris & Epstein 2017, Cacioppo et al. 1984, Riding 1991, Riding & Rayner 1998, Kirton 1976, von Wittich & Antonakis 2011, Sternberg 1988/1997, Sowden et al. 2014) — they were either redundant with verified sources, unverified against full-text, or not essential for the construct structure.
### 2.1 Structural sources (define what we measure)

- **Cacioppo and Petty (1982), Need for Cognition Scale (JPSP).** Four studies developing and validating the NFC. Factor analysis yielded ONE major factor — NFC is unidimensional. Items measure "the tendency for an individual to engage in and enjoy thinking" (p. 116). Unrelated to social desirability, weakly related to cognitive style, weakly negatively related to dogmatism, positively correlated with intelligence. Verified: items are entirely about enjoyment, not speed or ability. *Use:* core anchor for the C1 facet (Deliberation Preference). The unidimensionality finding means C1 and C2 are a cross-construct split, not a two-factor decomposition of NFC — stated in §2.5 honesty notes.

- **Cacioppo, Petty, Feinstein and Jarvis (1996), NFC meta-analysis (Psychological Bulletin).** Comprehensive review of the NFC construct across multiple samples and paradigms. Confirms NFC as a stable dispositional variable distinct from cognitive ability. *Use:* corroborates C1 and provides the evidence base that enjoyment-of-thinking is a real individual difference, not a transient state.

- **Epstein, Pacini, Denes-Raj and Heier (1996), Rational-Experiential Inventory (JPSP).** Two studies validating the REI. Factor analysis yielded TWO ORTHOGONAL factors corresponding to NFC (rational) and Faith in Intuition (FI, experiential). Correlation between the two: r = .08 — "largely independent" (p. 399). The 10-item short form (5 NFC + 5 FI) had α = .73/.72; at 8+ items the Spearman-Brown projection exceeds .85. *Use:* core anchor for Axis C (Processing Mode). The decisive finding is that rational and experiential are INDEPENDENT, not opposite poles — exactly the same pattern as Test 1's Axis B (approach/withdrawal per Carver & White). The implicature for our design is in the §2.5 honesty notes.

- **Frederick (2005), Cognitive Reflection Test (J. Economic Perspectives).** Three-item behavioral test measuring the ability to override an intuitive (but wrong) answer with a reflective one. CRT predicts decision-making biases above IQ. CRT is related to but distinct from NFC — enjoyment of thinking does not guarantee successful override. *Use:* behavioral-trait anchor for the C2 facet (Override Tendency). Does NOT provide self-report items — our C2 items are designed as dispositional proxies for the tendency to verify, not behavioral CRT problems. The construct distinction C1 ≠ C2 is stated in §2.5.

- **Stanovich and West (2000), Individual differences in reasoning (BBS).** Landmark target article (82 pp. + peer commentary). Establishes that thinking dispositions (NFC, AOT) predict reasoning performance above cognitive ability. The dual-process framework: System 1 (intuitive/automatic) vs. System 2 (analytic/decontextualized). "Cognitive decontextualization" — the ability to decouple prior beliefs from problem content — is the key mechanism. *Use:* provides the overarching individual-differences framework linking C1 (enjoyment of thinking) and C2 (verification tendency) to a single latent "engagement of System 2" interpretation.

- **Stanovich and West (1997), Actively Open-Minded Thinking (J. Educational Psychology).** Composite AOT scale (6 subscales: Flexible Thinking + Openness-Ideas + Openness-Values − Absolutism − Dogmatism − Categorical Thinking; α = .88). AOT predicts argument evaluation above cognitive ability. NOTE: two of six subscales are NEO-PI-R facets — AOT overlaps substantially with Big Five Openness. *Use:* supplementary corroboration that individual differences in cognitive processing exist above ability. Serves as texture for the result profiles (the "open-minded / flexible" shading across all four modes), not as a structural axis — AOT is more epistemic/personality than cognitive-style.

- **Riding (1997), On the nature of cognitive style (Educational Psychology).** Review of the Cognitive Styles Analysis. Two independent dimensions: Wholist-Analytic (r ≈ ±0.1 with Verbal-Imagery). Wholist-Analytic is independent of intelligence (correlations with ability subtests: r ≈ 0.00–0.04) and independent of personality. The CSA uses behavioral (reaction-time) assessment, not self-report. Riding explicitly criticizes self-report measures (p. 31: "inability to report accurately, unwillingness to make the necessary effort, social desirability bias") but acknowledges validated self-report instruments exist (Allinson & Hayes, 1996). *Use:* core anchor for Axis D (Encoding Structure), specifically the Wholist-Analytic (parts-first vs. whole-first) dimension. The CSA is behavioral; our conversion to self-report is a design choice stated in §2.5.

- **Nisbett, Peng, Choi and Norenzayan (2001), Culture and systems of thought (Psychological Review).** Cross-cultural validation of the holistic vs. analytic distinction. East Asians tend toward holistic (context/field-sensitive) processing; Westerners tend toward analytic (object/category-based) processing. The distinction maps onto perceptual field dependence/independence (Witkin). *Use:* independent, cross-cultural corroboration that the parts/wholes distinction is a genuine, stable cognitive dimension — not a measurement artifact of one instrument. Supplementary citation; does not provide item content or a two-facet structure.
### 2.2 Textural sources (define how we describe)
Each result's profile draws vocabulary from the broader cognitive-styles and thinking-dispositions literature. No textural source below is used as a structural anchor.

- **Sternberg (1988, 1997), Thinking Styles.** 13 thinking styles across functions, forms, levels, scopes. *Use:* archetype vocabulary for the result profiles only. Too many dimensions to structure a two-axis test, so not used structurally. NOTE: not verified against full-text; cited for naming richness only.
### 2.3 Why two axes, why these two, why not three

- **Why not three (Verbaliser-Imager).** Riding validates Verbaliser-Imager as orthogonal to Wholist-Analytic (r ≈ ±0.1). The dimension has genuine construct validity. We drop it because (a) it adds a third axis that breaks the suite's 4-quadrant template, (b) it overlaps with modality-of-study rather than core cognition, and (c) the suite template is locked (§2 of the framework doc). Wholist-Analytic is the more cognition-level construct.

- **Why not a creativity axis.** Creativity is a capability, not a cognitive mode. Sowden, Pringle and Gabora (2014) show creative generation and refinement map onto Type 1 and Type 2 processes, meaning creativity is distributed across all four quadrants. Forcing a creativity axis would conflate capability with style.

- **Why Epstein dual-process rather than MBTI thinking-vs-feeling.** Epstein treats rational and experiential as independent dimensions, confirmed as orthogonal in the full-text (r = .08). MBTI dichotomizes them. Same flaw as Test 1's rationale for rejecting MBTI (McCrae and Costa 1989).
### 2.4 Response-format sources (inherit from Test 1)
Decisions apply unchanged from Test 1. Full argument in `01-solstice-cycle-assessment.md` §7.
- **Sun, Schmidt and Henry (2025).** Sliders underperform Likert.
- **Chang (1994), Gosling et al. (2003), Spearman-Brown.** Seven points, eight items per axis.
- **McCrae and Costa (1989), Schulte et al. (2020).** Reject forced-choice and dichotomizing.
### 2.5 Facet grounding and honesty notes

The facets under each axis are grounded in validated constructs. Three honesty notes document design choices that deviate from the source instruments' structures — the same discipline Test 1 applies to Axis A compositing and the D1/D2 split.
**Axis C facets.**

- **C1 Deliberation Preference:** Cacioppo and Petty (1982) Need for Cognition. The tendency to engage in and enjoy effortful, analytical thinking. NFC is unidimensional (one major factor, 1982 Study 1). Items are entirely about enjoyment, not speed or ability (e.g., "I prefer complex to simple problems"; "Thinking is not my idea of fun" [R]).

- **C2 Override Tendency:** Frederick (2005) Cognitive Reflection Test, as dispositional proxy. The tendency to pause, verify, and check intuitions rather than trust the first answer. CRT is a behavioral test; our C2 items are designed as self-report dispositional proxies — not Frederick's items. Supported by Stanovich and West (2000) on "cognitive decontextualization" as the key System 2 operation.

**Honesty note 1 (Axis C compositing).** NFC (rational engagement) and FI (experiential intuition) are orthogonal in the REI (Epstein et al., 1996; r = .08, p < .001 but negligible effect size — "largely independent"). Treating them as a single bipolar axis is a design choice that collapses two dimensions into one. A mid-axis score can mean "high in both" (genuinely bimodal), "low in both" (disengaged), or genuinely balanced. The C1 and C2 facet sub-scores disambiguate: C1 (NFC-based) reflects the rational pole's contribution; a low C1 combined with a mid-range axis score suggests a bimodal profile (high in both NFC and FI), which the facet signature surfaces.

**Honesty note 2 (C1/C2 cross-construct split).** C1 maps to NFC, which Cacioppo and Petty (1982) found unidimensional. C2 maps to the dispositional side of cognitive override, which NFC items alone do not measure. The two facets share a latent "engagement of System 2" interpretation (Stanovich and West, 2000) but are NOT independently validated as a two-factor decomposition of a single construct. They are reported separately so any divergence (e.g., high enjoyment of thinking but low verification tendency) is visible. If pilot data shows them loading on a single factor, the separate reporting is harmless — their scores would simply converge.
**Axis D facets.**

- **D1 Entry Point:** Riding (1997) Wholist-Analytic dimension. What registers first when approaching new information — the parts or the whole? Riding treats Wholist-Analytic as unidimensional and uses behavioral (reaction-time) assessment via the CSA.

- **D2 Decomposition Habit:** Same Riding source, but applied to ongoing processing (not first entry). Do you decompose into units or synthesize into wholes once you have the information? D2 is our design extension, not Riding's.

**Honesty note 3 (D1/D2 designer decomposition, self-report conversion).** Riding (1997) treats Wholist-Analytic as unidimensional and assesses it behaviorally via reaction-time tasks. Our split into D1 (entry) and D2 (ongoing processing) applies DeYoung's two-aspect pattern to a cognitive-style dimension with no jointly validated two-factor structure. Our self-report Likert format converts Riding's behavioral CSA construct to self-report items — a conversion Riding himself flags (p. 31) as having inherent weaknesses ("inability to report accurately, unwillingness to make the effort, social desirability bias"). Both choices are transparent: D1/D2 are reported separately; if they prove to be a single factor, the split is harmless; the self-report format carries the same limitations as every other test in this suite and is stated in §10.

**Honesty note 4 (Axis C/Openness overlap).** Deliberation Preference (C1) overlaps with Big Five Openness-to-Ideas (confirmed in Stanovich & West, 1997: the Openness-Ideas NEO-PI-R facet loads on the AOT composite). Override Tendency (C2) overlaps with Conscientiousness's deliberation facet. Wholist-Analytic (Axis D) overlaps weakly with Openness. These are validated constructs we build on, not inventions. The MMA's contribution is the combination, the facet structure, and the cognitive (not personality) framing.
## 3. Why the framework fits the Turing theme

Turing's core insight was that there are many valid ways a mind can compute. The Imitation Game asks whether a hidden mind can be inferred from its outputs. The MMA asks the inverse: given your outputs (your item responses), which mode of mind is yours?

The fit is structural. Turing's own work spans all four quadrants — not as a retrospective mapping, but as a direct correspondence between the cognitive mode each quadrant describes and what Turing actually built or discovered:
| Turing's work | Cognitive mode | Why the fit is genuine, not decorative |

| The Turing Machine, the Halting Problem (1936) | ⚙️ The Algorithm (sequential + deliberate) | Turing formalized computation as a deterministic sequence of exact operations. The Algorithm is the mode this formalization describes: stepwise, verifiable, each operation justified by the one before it. The Turing Machine IS the operational definition of sequential+deliberate. |

| Enigma codebreaking, Bombe design (1939–42) | 🕸️ The Cipher (sequential + intuitive) | Cryptanalysis involves sequential operation (character by character, frequency by frequency) driven by pattern recognition rather than formal proof. The Bombe automated this: an electro-mechanical pattern-matcher that tested rotor settings against known cribs. The mapping is to the cognitive mode of the activity, not to Turing's personal style — the weakest of the four mappings, stated openly. |

| Morphogenesis, reaction-diffusion (1952) | 🔮 The Gestalt (holistic + intuitive) | Turing's morphogenesis paper describes how global patterns (spots, stripes, spirals) emerge from simple local rules — the definition of a holistic+intuitive insight. He saw the whole pattern arising from the system dynamics, not from specifying each element. This is the purest expression of the Gestalt mode. |

| ACE architecture, computability theory (1945) | 🏗️ The Architecture (holistic + deliberate) | The ACE design was a complete system architecture — Turing designed the whole machine, not a component. His computability work asks what can be computed in principle, a systems-level question approached with formal rigor. The Architecture mode: deliberate, structured, and about wholes. |

The test's framing: *Turing showed that minds, like machines, come in different architectures. Which of these is yours?* The mapping is structural and historically grounded, not decorative. The one mapping that stretches (the Cipher → Enigma via the mode of the activity, not the man) is stated openly rather than implied.
**Axis C, Processing Mode** (how you arrive at answers).
- Construct basis: Cacioppo & Petty (1982) Need for Cognition. Epstein et al. (1996) REI. Frederick (2005) CRT (behavioral anchor for C2). Stanovich & West (2000) dual-process framework.
- High pole, Deliberate (System 2): effortful, analytical, and enjoys the thinking itself — not just the answer. The NFC core.
- Low pole, Intuitive (System 1): rapid, automatic, pattern-based, low-effort. Reframed as fluency and speed, never as laziness or error.

- **Honesty note (full-text verified).** NFC and Faith in Intuition are orthogonal in the REI (Epstein et al., 1996; r = .08). Treating them as a single bipolar axis is a design choice. A mid-axis score may reflect being high in both, low in both, or genuinely intermediate. The C1 and C2 facet sub-scores disambiguate. See §2.5.
**Axis D, Encoding Structure** (how you take in and structure information).
- Construct basis: Riding (1997) Wholist-Analytic dimension. Nisbett et al. (2001) cross-cultural corroboration.
- High pole, Sequential: parts-first, ordered, builds bottom-up.
- Low pole, Holistic: whole-first, configurational, builds top-down. Neither pole is superior.

- **Honesty note (full-text verified).** Riding's CSA assesses Wholist-Analytic behaviorally (reaction time), not via self-report. Our conversion to self-report Likert is a design choice. The D1/D2 split into Entry Point and Decomposition Habit is a designer decomposition of a unidimensional construct — see §2.5.
## 6. Methodology and scoring
Inherits Test 1's model identically — the math is construct-agnostic and applies to any two-axis continuous instrument.
**Step 1, collect.** 32 responses, each 1 to 7. Four facets (C1, C2, D1, D2), 8 items each.
**Step 2, direction-normalize.** Map each item so a higher value always means more Deliberate (Axis C) or more Sequential (Axis D). Reverse-keyed items are inverted.
**Step 3, facet scores.** C1 = mean of normalized C1 items, scaled 0–100. Similarly for C2, D1, D2.
**Step 4, axis scores.** C = mean of C1 and C2, 0–100 (0 = Intuitive, 100 = Deliberate). D = mean of D1 and D2, 0–100 (0 = Holistic, 100 = Sequential).
**Step 5, locate on the plane.** Center is (50, 50). Quadrant from the signs of C−50 and D−50.
- C>50, D>50: The Algorithm
- C<50, D>50: The Cipher
- C<50, D<50: The Gestalt
- C>50, D<50: The Architecture
- Prototypicality r = distance from center / 70.7.
- Phase angle = atan2(D−50, C−50). Used for gradation.

- Gradation convention. Same cycle-tracking logic as Test 1. Progress through each quadrant is measured from the entry edge (the boundary with the adjacent quadrant in the natural rotation of the two axes). Binned Early (0–30°), Mid (30–60°), Late (60–90°).
**Step 6, classify.** Facet-tension detection and result assignment follow Test 1's v0.19 model exactly.
- Facet-tension check. An axis is tense when its two facets sit on opposite sides of 50 and both are at least 20 points from 50 (designer-set, tunable) — the signature of cancellation.
- r ≥ 0.28 and no tense axis: report primary mode plus gradation plus leaning, plus the facet signature. If an axis is tense, the mode is still reported but carries a facet-tension modifier.

- r < 0.28 and no tense axis: report **The Halting Point** — the boundary condition, genuinely balanced. The name references Turing's Halting Problem: a formal undecidability result in which no algorithm can determine in general whether a program will terminate. Similarly, a near-center respondent's mode cannot be definitively reduced to a single quadrant — but this is not a failure; it is a structurally honest answer. (Formerly "Undecidable" in v0.2.)

- r < 0.28 with at least one tense axis: same Halting Point boundary, but with the facet-tension modifier rewriting the narrative from "balanced" to "holding opposites, led by the facet signature." This is not a new result type — it is the boundary condition with its narrative rewritten by the modifier.

This is the hybrid dimensional and prototypical pattern (Kerber et al., 2021) inherited from Test 1. It avoids the midpoint cliff (McCrae and Costa, 1989). The Halting Point, like the Threshold in Test 1, is a boundary condition — not a fifth type.
## 8. Item bank, facets, and lengths

**Two lengths, one item bank.** The MMA is offered as a 32-item standard form (MMA-32) and a 16-item short form (MMA-16) drawn from the same bank. Both share the same scoring model and result taxonomy. MMA-32 is the default; MMA-16 is a screening-tier quick read (4 items per facet, Spearman-Brown α ≈ .60–.70 — the same marginal band SCA-16 sits in, stated openly).
**Facet structure.**

- Axis C, Processing Mode: **C1 Deliberation Preference** (enjoyment of effortful thinking, Need for Cognition core), **C2 Override Tendency** (checking and verifying intuitions, Cognitive Reflection dispositional proxy). C1 maps to NFC (Cacioppo & Petty, 1982); C2 maps to the dispositional side of CRT (Frederick, 2005). They share a latent "System 2 engagement" interpretation (Stanovich & West, 2000) but are NOT a validated two-factor decomposition — see §2.5 honesty note 2.

- Axis D, Encoding Structure: **D1 Entry Point** (what registers first — parts or whole), **D2 Decomposition Habit** (ongoing: decompose or synthesize). Both draw from Riding's (1997) unidimensional Wholist-Analytic. The split is our design choice — see §2.5 honesty note 3.

**Item-writing rules applied.** Vary exactly one facet per item. No C items with D framing, no D items with C language. True antonym poles on a single dimension. Neutral language (behavior, not virtue). No transparent giveaways. Gender-neutral and identity-agnostic. Both poles affirming. Pole direction randomized at render time.
### Facet C1: Deliberation Preference (8 items)

All items vary enjoyment of and preference for effortful thinking. No encoding-structure language, no speed/ability framing. Content areas drawn from NFC items (Cacioppo & Petty, 1982; Epstein et al., 1996): problem enjoyment, understanding vs. efficiency, thinking as fulfillment, thinking as default mode.
| # | Scenario stem | Deliberate pole (System 2) | Intuitive pole (System 1) |
| C1.1 | How often do you enjoy effortful, slow thinking for its own sake? | "Often. I like grinding through a hard problem." | "Rarely. I'd rather get to the answer and move on." |
| C1.2 | When you're learning something new, you prefer to… | "Understand the principles first, deliberately." | "Pick it up by doing, before I have the theory." |
| C1.3 | When a problem makes you think hard for an extended time, you feel… | "Energized. This is why I'm here." | "Drained. I'd rather be done." |
| C1.4 | A hard problem lands on you. Your impulse is to… | "Sit with it and work it through." | "Find the quickest path to an answer." |
| C1.5 | You'd rather… | "Spend an hour understanding why." | "Spend an hour getting it done." |
| C1.6 | Thinking hard feels… | "Satisfying. I seek it out." | "Costly. I'd rather avoid it." |
| C1.7 | When something is complex… | "I want to map it fully before acting." | "I want to get the gist and act." |
| C1.8 | Effortful reasoning is… | "My natural mode." | "Something I use only when I must." |

v0.3 note: C1.3 replaced. The v0.2 item "Your natural speed for hard problems" framed the construct as speed, not enjoyment — NFC items deliberately avoid speed framing (Cacioppo & Petty, 1982). Replaced with an enjoyment-vs-drain framing mapped from NFC items ("I find little satisfaction in deliberating hard" [R]; "I really enjoy a task that involves coming up with new solutions").
### Facet C2: Override Tendency (8 items)

All items vary how much you check or verify intuitions before trusting them. Not about preference for thinking — that is C1. Content areas: initial-impulse verification, gut-vs-analysis conflict, tolerance for unexplained knowledge, verification as default vs. exception.
| # | Scenario stem | Deliberate pole (verifies) | Intuitive pole (trusts fast) |
| C2.1 | You get an answer quickly and it feels right. What do you do? | "Slow down and verify it before trusting it." | "Trust it, then move on." |
| C2.2 | A gut feeling conflicts with your analysis. You tend to… | "Follow the analysis." | "Follow the gut, even if I can't justify it yet." |
| C2.3 | When you can't explain how you know something, you… | "Don't fully trust it until I can." | "Trust it anyway. Some knowledge is pre-verbal." |
| C2.4 | Your first instinct on a question is usually… | "A hypothesis I then check." | "Something I trust and run with." |
| C2.5 | When you're confident fast… | "I still want to verify." | "I act on it." |
| C2.6 | When you make a snap judgment… | "I usually circle back and check it later." | "I trust it and move on." |
| C2.7 | Doubt, for you, is… | "A signal to dig deeper." | "A drag I'd rather skip." |
| C2.8 | When the stakes are real… | "I override instinct with analysis." | "I trust instinct and analyze after." |

v0.3 note: C2.6 replaced. The v0.2 item "A quick judgment you made gets re-examined if I have time" confounded disposition with opportunity (the "if I have time" conditional makes it state-dependent rather than dispositional). Replaced with a dispositional frame: "I usually circle back and check" — the tendency, not the circumstance.
### Facet D1: Entry Point (8 items)
All items vary what registers first when you approach new information. No processing-mode words.
| # | Scenario stem | Sequential pole (parts-first) | Holistic pole (whole-first) |
| D1.1 | You're handed a problem you've never seen before. First move? | "Break it into steps and solve each one." | "Get the overall shape of it, then fill in." |
| D1.2 | How do you usually grasp a new idea? | "Component by component, until the whole assembles." | "Whole first, then I learn what the parts are." |
| D1.3 | When you read, your eye moves… | "Line by line, in order." | "Around the page, grabbing the shape of it first." |
| D1.4 | A new subject. You start with… | "The basics, the building blocks." | "The big picture, what it's about." |
| D1.5 | Entering a new situation… | "I notice the pieces first." | "I get the overall feel first." |
| D1.6 | When learning a new skill, you start with… | "The individual techniques, one at a time." | "Understanding what the skill feels like as a whole." |
| D1.7 | When information arrives… | "I take it in piece by piece." | "I take in the whole pattern." |
| D1.8 | Your entry point into anything new is… | "The parts." | "The whole." |

v0.3 note: D1.6 replaced. The v0.2 item "A new person… I register details about them / I get an overall impression" was a near-duplicate of D1.5 ("entering a new situation") — both measured entry point via situational frame. Replaced with a learning-domain frame ("learning a new skill") to extend content coverage across contexts without creating an overlapping confound.
### Facet D2: Decomposition Habit (8 items)

All items vary how you work with information once you have it — ongoing processing: decompose into units or synthesize into wholes. Distinct from D1 (first entry): D1 is the moment of encountering; D2 is the habit of working.
| # | Scenario stem | Sequential pole (decomposes) | Holistic pole (synthesizes) |
| D2.1 | You're explaining something you understand well. You tend to… | "Build it up piece by piece for the listener." | "Give the whole picture first, then refine." |
| D2.2 | A complex system is in front of you. Where do you start? | "With the individual components and how each works." | "With the overall structure and what it's doing." |
| D2.3 | You're designing something from scratch. You… | "Work through the components in sequence." | "Hold the complete vision in mind, then realize it." |
| D2.4 | A pile of details lands on you. You prefer to… | "Order them into a sequence and work through it." | "Stand back and find the pattern they form." |
| D2.5 | When the details don't add up to a sensible whole, you… | "Keep working the parts until they do." | "Step back and reconsider the shape of the whole." |
| D2.6 | Faced with complexity… | "I decompose it into manageable units." | "I look for the unifying pattern." |
| D2.7 | Your instinct with any system… | "Take it apart to understand it." | "Find what holds it together." |
| D2.8 | Understanding, for you, comes from… | "Assembling parts into wholes." | "Grasping wholes that contain their parts." |

v0.3 note: D2.3 replaced. The v0.2 item "You're building something (a meal, a design, a doc)" was double-barreled in its example domain (three concrete domains with different cognitive demands). Replaced with a single-domain frame ("designing something from scratch") for item unidimensionality.

**Notes.** All 32 items are gender-neutral and identity-agnostic. Both poles of every item are affirming. A launch pass should run an internal-consistency check per facet and drop or replace the weakest 1 to 2 items if any facet alpha falls below .75. The four items replaced in v0.3 (C1.3, C2.6, D1.6, D2.3) were fixed for construct alignment against the full-text papers; they have not been pilot-tested.

**Overlap honesty.** Axis C (Processing Mode) overlaps with Big Five Openness-to-Ideas (via C1, confirmed in Stanovich & West, 1997) and Conscientiousness (via C2's deliberation/responsibility shading). Axis D (Encoding Structure) overlaps weakly with Openness. These are validated constructs we build on, not inventions. The MMA's contribution is the combination, the facet structure, and the cognitive (not personality) framing.
### 8.1 The 16-item short form (MMA-16)

Same subset approach as SCA-16: curated selection of 4 items per facet from the 32-item bank, content-driven (no pilot data), screening-tier reliability (.60–.70 alpha band), with the short-form caveat on results. Selection TBD after the full-bank audit is complete — the four items replaced in v0.3 need to settle before selection. Follows the same pattern and honesty tier as `01-solstice-cycle-assessment.md` §8.1.
## 9. Interpretation and reporting
A result has four layers, surfaced in order:
1. **Your mode** (quadrant). The shareable label.
2. **Your position** (angle). Gradation and secondary leaning.

3. **Your prototypicality** (radius). Strongly versus with nuance. Near-center yields **The Halting Point** — the boundary condition, named for Turing's formal undecidability result. Its narrative splits depending on the facet-tension modifier: genuinely balanced ("no algorithm can settle this") or holding opposites ("two strong facets cancel, not balance").

4. **Your narrative.** Two to three personalized paragraphs from the full answer pattern, ending with a "your halting point" line (the Turing-flavored equivalent of Test 1's "your moment on the cycle"). Gemini layer per the GDD.

**Deterministic fallback (no-API path).** 12 seasonal-mode states (4 modes × {early, mid, late}) plus the Halting Point boundary reading (two narrative variants via the facet-tension modifier). The type count is four; the Halting Point is a boundary condition, not a fifth type. The game is fully playable without the API.
**Never reported as:** an IQ score, a creativity score, a competence ranking, a fixed identity, or a clinical assessment.
**Limitations, stated up front in the product.**
- Not a validated clinical instrument. Inspired by validated models (NFC, REI, CRT, Wholist-Analytic). Not independently psychometrically evaluated.
- Self-report biases remain. Mitigated, not eliminated, by scenario framing and Likert format. Riding (1997) specifically notes self-report weaknesses for cognitive style.

- The REI dimensions (NFC and FI) are orthogonal (Epstein et al., 1996). Collapsing them into one bipolar axis loses information — the facet signature recovers some, not all, of the lost texture. See §2.5 honesty note 1.
- The mode names are interpretive. We measure processing preference and encoding structure. We name the result computationally.

- The Halting Problem reference is a metaphor. Formal undecidability is a proof about Turing machines, not about cognitive profiles. The metaphor is made explicit so it is not mistaken for a formal claim.
- State versus trait ambiguity. The MMA blurs stable disposition with current thinking habits. We lean into this, but it is not a pure trait measure.
## 11. Status
Test 2 v0.3. Updated for parity with Test 1's v0.19 standard.
- Name locked: The Modes of Mind Assessment (MMA).
- Result naming locked: mode-primary with archetype subtitle (`⚙️ The Algorithm`).
- Boundary renamed: Undecidable → The Halting Point.
- Suite template applied. Scoring model, facet-tension detection, gradation convention, and modifier flag port directly from Test 1.
- Four items replaced (C1.3, C2.6, D1.6, D2.3) for construct alignment against full-text paper content.
- Citations audited: kept only sources with verified full-text; dropped 8 redundant or unverified citations.

- Three honesty notes added (§2.5) documenting the NFC/FI compositing, C1/C2 cross-construct split, and D1/D2 designer decomposition — following Test 1's pattern of transparently stating where the framework deviates from source instruments.
- Short form (MMA-16, 4 per facet) documented in §8.1. Selection TBD pending the full bank audit.
- Profiles, debug build, and simulation deferred to the next pass.
See `CHANGELOG.md` for revision history.

+ 55#KS:### 2.5 Facet grounding and honesty notes
+ 56#XN:
+ 57#YJ:The facets under each axis are grounded in validated constructs. Three honesty notes document design choices that deviate from the source instruments' structures — the same discipline Test 1 applies to Axis A compositing and the D1/D2 split.
+ 58#KR:
+ 59#QN:**Axis C facets.**
+ 60#BN:- **C1 Deliberation Preference:** Cacioppo and Petty (1982) Need for Cognition. The tendency to engage in and enjoy effortful, analytical thinking. NFC is unidimensional (one major factor, 1982 Study 1). Items are entirely about enjoyment, not speed or ability (e.g., "I prefer complex to simple problems"; "Thinking is not my idea of fun" [R]).
+ 61#YN:- **C2 Override Tendency:** Frederick (2005) Cognitive Reflection Test, as dispositional proxy. The tendency to pause, verify, and check intuitions rather than trust the first answer. CRT is a behavioral test; our C2 items are designed as self-report dispositional proxies — not Frederick's items. Supported by Stanovich and West (2000) on "cognitive decontextualization" as the key System 2 operation.
+ 62#RJ:
+ 63#TJ:**Honesty note 1 (Axis C compositing).** NFC (rational engagement) and FI (experiential intuition) are orthogonal in the REI (Epstein et al., 1996; r = .08, p < .001 but negligible effect size — "largely independent"). Treating them as a single bipolar axis is a design choice that collapses two dimensions into one. A mid-axis score can mean "high in both" (genuinely bimodal), "low in both" (disengaged), or genuinely balanced. The C1 and C2 facet sub-scores disambiguate: C1 (NFC-based) reflects the rational pole's contribution; a low C1 combined with a mid-range axis score suggests a bimodal profile (high in both NFC and FI), which the facet signature surfaces.
+ 64#XZ:
+ 65#HH:**Honesty note 2 (C1/C2 cross-construct split).** C1 maps to NFC, which Cacioppo and Petty (1982) found unidimensional. C2 maps to the dispositional side of cognitive override, which NFC items alone do not measure. The two facets share a latent "engagement of System 2" interpretation (Stanovich and West, 2000) but are NOT independently validated as a two-factor decomposition of a single construct. They are reported separately so any divergence (e.g., high enjoyment of thinking but low verification tendency) is visible. If pilot data shows them loading on a single factor, the separate reporting is harmless — their scores would simply converge.
+ 66#JQ:
+ 67#ZB:**Axis D facets.**
+ 68#QV:- **D1 Entry Point:** Riding (1997) Wholist-Analytic dimension. What registers first when approaching new information — the parts or the whole? Riding treats Wholist-Analytic as unidimensional and uses behavioral (reaction-time) assessment via the CSA.
+ 69#ZK:- **D2 Decomposition Habit:** Same Riding source, but applied to ongoing processing (not first entry). Do you decompose into units or synthesize into wholes once you have the information? D2 is our design extension, not Riding's.
+ 70#YY:
+ 71#PN:**Honesty note 3 (D1/D2 designer decomposition, self-report conversion).** Riding (1997) treats Wholist-Analytic as unidimensional and assesses it behaviorally via reaction-time tasks. Our split into D1 (entry) and D2 (ongoing processing) applies DeYoung's two-aspect pattern to a cognitive-style dimension with no jointly validated two-factor structure. Our self-report Likert format converts Riding's behavioral CSA construct to self-report items — a conversion Riding himself flags (p. 31) as having inherent weaknesses ("inability to report accurately, unwillingness to make the effort, social desirability bias"). Both choices are transparent: D1/D2 are reported separately; if they prove to be a single factor, the split is harmless; the self-report format carries the same limitations as every other test in this suite and is stated in §10.
+ 72#SV:
+ 73#RZ:**Honesty note 4 (Axis C/Openness overlap).** Deliberation Preference (C1) overlaps with Big Five Openness-to-Ideas (confirmed in Stanovich & West, 1997: the Openness-Ideas NEO-PI-R facet loads on the AOT composite). Override Tendency (C2) overlaps with Conscientiousness's deliberation facet. Wholist-Analytic (Axis D) overlaps weakly with Openness. These are validated constructs we build on, not inventions. The MMA's contribution is the combination, the facet structure, and the cognitive (not personality) framing.

  90#QT:
- 60    Turing's core insight was that there are many valid ways a mind can compute. The Imitation Game asks whether a hidden mind can be inferred from its outputs. The MMA asks the inverse: given your outputs, which mode of mind is yours?

- 62    The fit is structural. Turing's own work spans all four quadrants, which lets each result name point at a real piece of his legacy:
+ 93#XS:The fit is structural. Turing's own work spans all four quadrants — not as a retrospective mapping, but as a direct correspondence between the cognitive mode each quadrant describes and what Turing actually built or discovered:

- 65    |---|---|
- 66    | The Turing Machine, the Halting Problem | ⚙️ The Algorithm (sequential + deliberate) |
- 67    | Enigma codebreaking, Bombe design | 🕸️ The Cipher (sequential + intuitive pattern work) |
- 68    | Morphogenesis, reaction-diffusion | 🔮 The Gestalt (holistic + intuitive emergence) |

+ 96#HZ:|---|---|---|
+ 97#HV:| The Turing Machine, the Halting Problem (1936) | ⚙️ The Algorithm (sequential + deliberate) | Turing formalized computation as a deterministic sequence of exact operations. The Algorithm is the mode this formalization describes: stepwise, verifiable, each operation justified by the one before it. The Turing Machine IS the operational definition of sequential+deliberate. |
+ 98#XQ:| Enigma codebreaking, Bombe design (1939–42) | 🕸️ The Cipher (sequential + intuitive) | Cryptanalysis involves sequential operation (character by character, frequency by frequency) driven by pattern recognition rather than formal proof. The Bombe automated this: an electro-mechanical pattern-matcher that tested rotor settings against known cribs. The mapping is to the cognitive mode of the activity, not to Turing's personal style — the weakest of the four mappings, stated openly. |

lines: ## v0.3 (2026-06-19): Test 2 full-text paper audit, citations updated, Turing theme verified

Why: the v0.2 design cited 13+ cognitive psychology sources but the paper-downloads folder contained one verified cognitive paper (Stanovich & West, 2000). Seven new full-text PDFs were acquired and reviewed, and the design was rebuilt against what the papers actually say, not what the v0.2 citations claimed.
### Papers reviewed (full-text, not abstracts)
- Cacioppo & Petty (1982), NFC Scale. NFC is unidimensional (one major factor). Items are entirely about enjoyment, not speed or ability.
- Cacioppo et al. (1996), NFC meta-analysis. Confirms NFC as a stable disposition distinct from ability.

- Epstein et al. (1996), REI. Two ORTHOGONAL factors (NFC and Faith in Intuition; r = .08). Rational and experiential are independent, not opposite poles — a person can be high in both or low in both.
- Frederick (2005), CRT. Three behavioral items. CRT is related to but distinct from NFC — enjoyment of thinking does not guarantee successful override.

- Riding (1997), Cognitive Styles Analysis. Wholist-Analytic is unidimensional, independent of IQ and personality, assessed behaviorally (reaction-time). Riding explicitly criticizes self-report measures.
- Stanovich & West (1997), AOT. Composite of 6 subscales (α = .88). Overlaps NEO-PI-R Openness (two subscales are NEO-PI-R facets).
- Nisbett et al. (2001). Cross-cultural validation of the holistic/analytic distinction. Confirms the parts/wholes divide is a genuine, stable cognitive dimension.
- Stanovich & West (2000) was already in hand from Test 1.
### Key findings that changed the design

**Axis C compositing honesty note.** The REI confirms NFC and FI are orthogonal. Treating them as a single bipolar Processing Mode axis composites two independent dimensions — the same pattern as Test 1's Axis A. A mid-axis score can mean "high in both," "low in both," or genuinely intermediate; the C1/C2 facet scores disambiguate. Honesty note added to §2.5 and §4.

**C1/C2 cross-construct split.** C1 maps to NFC, which is unidimensional (Cacioppo & Petty, 1982). C2 maps to the dispositional side of CRT (Frederick, 2005) — a different construct. The split is across constructs, not a validated two-factor decomposition of one. Honesty note added.

**D1/D2 designer decomposition.** Riding treats Wholist-Analytic as unidimensional and assesses it behaviorally. Our D1/D2 split and self-report format are design choices, not Riding's. Riding explicitly criticizes self-report for cognitive style. Honesty note added.

**Citations pruned.** Eight sources dropped from v0.2 (Pacini 1999; Norris & Epstein 2017; Cacioppo et al. 1984; Riding 1991; Riding & Rayner 1998; Kirton 1976; von Wittich & Antonakis 2011; Sternberg 1988/1997) — either redundant with verified sources, unverified against full-text, or not essential to the construct structure. Four new sources added with verified full-text (Cacioppo et al. 1996; Stanovich & West 1997; Nisbett et al. 2001; and Epstein et al. 1996 upgraded from cited to verified).
### Four items replaced for construct alignment against paper findings

- **C1.3.** v0.2 item "Your natural speed for hard problems" framed the construct as speed, not enjoyment. NFC items deliberately avoid speed framing (Cacioppo & Petty, 1982). Replaced with an enjoyment-vs-drain framing: "When a problem makes you think hard for an extended time, you feel energized / drained."

- **C2.6.** v0.2 item "A quick judgment you made gets re-examined if I have time" confounded disposition with opportunity (the "if I have time" conditional). Replaced with a dispositional frame: "When you make a snap judgment, I usually circle back and check it later / I trust it and move on."

- **D1.6.** v0.2 item "A new person — I register details about them first" was a near-duplicate of D1.5 ("entering a new situation"). Replaced with a learning-domain frame to extend content coverage: "When learning a new skill, you start with the individual techniques / understanding what the skill feels like as a whole."
- **D2.3.** v0.2 item "You're building something (a meal, a design, a doc)" was double-barreled in its example domain. Replaced with a single-domain frame: "You're designing something from scratch."
### Turing theme evaluation
Each mapping was verified against Turing's actual work:
- Algorithm → Turing Machine: STRONG. The 1936 paper formalized computation as a deterministic sequence.
- Cipher → Enigma: ADEQUATE. Maps to the cognitive mode of cryptanalysis (sequential + pattern recognition), not Turing's personal style. The weakest mapping; stated openly.
- Gestalt → Morphogenesis: STRONG. The 1952 paper describes global patterns emerging from local rules — the definition of holistic+intuitive.
- Architecture → ACE/computability: STRONG. ACE was a complete system architecture; computability asks what can be computed in principle — deliberate, holistic, systems-level.
No result names or mappings changed. The theme is substantially genuine, not superficial.
### Other updates

- Boundary renamed Undecidable → **The Halting Point**. The Halting Problem is about formal undecidability — a more precise Turing reference, and "Undecidable" had negative everyday shading. The Halting Point is a boundary condition, not a tier.
- Scoring section (v0.2 → v0.3) updated to match Test 1's v0.19 model: gradation convention, facet-tension detection, boundary classification, and the tension modifier flag.
- Short form (MMA-16, 4 per facet, screening-tier) documented in §8.1. Selection TBD pending the full bank audit.
- Profiles (02b): boundary-row updated to The Halting Point. Full profiles not yet re-audited (deferred).
### Files modified
- docs/02-modes-of-mind-assessment.md (v0.2 → v0.3)
- docs/02b-modes-result-profiles.md (Halting Point rename; modulation table)
- docs/CHANGELOG.md (this entry)
### Deferred

- Full item-bank audit (content-area mapping, construct purity across all 32 items — this pass addressed the four paper-explicit issues in C1.3, C2.6, D1.6, D2.3; the remaining 28 items need the same rigor pass Test 1 got across v0.12–v0.17).
- MMA-16 item selection.
- Profile re-audit (the 14-section profiles exist in 02b but haven't been through the rigor cycle).
- Build (`mma-debug.html`) and simulation (`mma-simulate.ts`).

edits.lines: > Honesty statement: The MMA is an original, theory-informed assessment for reflection and play. Its two axes are grounded in full-text-verified constructs: Processing Mode draws from Need for Cognition (Cacioppo & Petty, 1982), the Rational-Experiential Inventory (Epstein et al., 1996), and Cognitive Reflection (Frederick, 2005); Encoding Structure draws from Riding's (1997) Wholist-Analytic dimension, with cross-cultural corroboration from Nisbett et al. (2001). It is not independently validated and is not clinical. The four result names are an interpretive metaphor drawn from computing and Turing's own work, not a claim that human minds are literally algorithms.
**The Modes of Mind Assessment (MMA).**
Sources below are retained because full-text PDFs confirm the claimed use.

All items vary how you work with information once you have it — ongoing processing: decompose into units or synthesize into wholes. Distinct from D1 (first entry): D1 is the moment of encountering; D2 is the habit of working.

  26#VK:- **Cacioppo and Petty (1982), Need for Cognition Scale (JPSP).** Four studies developing and validating the NFC. Factor analysis yielded ONE major factor — NFC is unidimensional. Unrelated to social desirability, weakly related to cognitive style, weakly negatively related to dogmatism, positively correlated with intelligence. Verified: items are entirely about enjoyment, not speed or ability. *Use:* core anchor for the C1 facet (Deliberation Preference). The unidimensionality finding means C1 and C2 are a cross-construct split, not a two-factor decomposition of NFC — stated in §2.5 honesty notes.
  27#RJ:- **Cacioppo, Petty, Feinstein and Jarvis (1996), NFC meta-analysis (Psychological Bulletin).** Comprehensive review of the NFC construct across multiple samples and paradigms. Confirms NFC as a stable dispositional variable distinct from cognitive ability. *Use:* corroborates C1 and provides the evidence base that enjoyment-of-thinking is a real individual difference, not a transient state.
  28#HJ:- **Epstein, Pacini, Denes-Raj and Heier (1996), Rational-Experiential Inventory (JPSP).** Two studies validating the REI. Factor analysis yielded TWO ORTHOGONAL factors corresponding to NFC (rational) and Faith in Intuition (FI, experiential). Correlation between the two: r = .08 — "largely independent" (p. 399). The 10-item short form (5 NFC + 5 FI) had α = .73/.72; at 8+ items the Spearman-Brown projection exceeds .85. *Use:* core anchor for Axis C (Processing Mode). The decisive finding is that rational and experiential are INDEPENDENT, not opposite poles — exactly the same pattern as Test 1's Axis B (approach/withdrawal per Carver & White). The implicature for our design is in the §2.5 honesty notes.
  29#KB:- **Frederick (2005), Cognitive Reflection Test (J. Economic Perspectives).** Three-item behavioral test measuring the ability to override an intuitive (but wrong) answer with a reflective one. CRT predicts decision-making biases above IQ. CRT is related to but distinct from NFC — enjoyment of thinking does not guarantee successful override. *Use:* behavioral-trait anchor for the C2 facet (Override Tendency). Does NOT provide self-report items — our C2 items are designed as dispositional proxies for the tendency to verify, not behavioral CRT problems. The construct distinction C1 ≠ C2 is stated in §2.5.
  30#PW:- **Stanovich and West (2000), Individual differences in reasoning (BBS).** Landmark target article (82 pp. + peer commentary). Establishes that thinking dispositions (NFC, AOT) predict reasoning performance above cognitive ability. The dual-process framework: System 1 (intuitive/automatic) vs. System 2 (analytic/decontextualized). "Cognitive decontextualization" — the ability to decouple prior beliefs from problem content — is the key mechanism. *Use:* provides the overarching individual-differences framework linking C1 (enjoyment of thinking) and C2 (verification tendency) to a single latent "engagement of System 2" interpretation.
  31#YM:- **Stanovich and West (1997), Actively Open-Minded Thinking (J. Educational Psychology).** Composite AOT scale (6 subscales: Flexible Thinking + Openness-Ideas + Openness-Values − Absolutism − Dogmatism − Categorical Thinking; α = .88). AOT predicts argument evaluation above cognitive ability. NOTE: two of six subscales are NEO-PI-R facets — AOT overlaps substantially with Big Five Openness. *Use:* supplementary corroboration that individual differences in cognitive processing exist above ability. Serves as texture for the result profiles (the "open-minded / flexible" shading across all four modes), not as a structural axis — AOT is more epistemic/personality than cognitive-style.

They are reported separately so any divergence (e.g., high enjoyment of thinking but low verification tendency) is visible.
