  91#SK:## 3. Why the framework fits the Turing theme
  92#JZ:
  93#ZX:Turing's core insight was that there are many valid ways a mind can compute. The Imitation Game asks whether a hidden mind can be inferred from its outputs. The MMA asks the inverse: given your outputs (your item responses), which mode of mind is yours?
  94#MS:
  95#XS:The fit is structural. Turing's own work spans all four quadrants — not as a retrospective mapping, but as a direct correspondence between the cognitive mode each quadrant describes and what Turing actually built or discovered:
  96#ZT:
  97#BZ:| Turing's work | Cognitive mode | Why the fit is genuine, not decorative |
  98#PZ:|---|---|---|
  99#HV:| The Turing Machine, the Halting Problem (1936) | ⚙️ The Algorithm (sequential + deliberate) | Turing formalized computation as a deterministic sequence of exact operations. The Algorithm is the mode this formalization describes: stepwise, verifiable, each operation justified by the one before it. The Turing Machine IS the operational definition of sequential+deliberate. |
 100#XQ:| Enigma codebreaking, Bombe design (1939–42) | 🕸️ The Cipher (sequential + intuitive) | Cryptanalysis involves sequential operation (character by character, frequency by frequency) driven by pattern recognition rather than formal proof. The Bombe automated this: an electro-mechanical pattern-matcher that tested rotor settings against known cribs. The mapping is to the cognitive mode of the activity, not to Turing's personal style — the weakest of the four mappings, stated openly. |
 101#QY:| Morphogenesis, reaction-diffusion (1952) | 🔮 The Gestalt (holistic + intuitive) | Turing's morphogenesis paper describes how global patterns (spots, stripes, spirals) emerge from simple local rules — the definition of a holistic+intuitive insight. He saw the whole pattern arising from the system dynamics, not from specifying each element. This is the purest expression of the Gestalt mode. |
 102#ZJ:| ACE architecture, computability theory (1945) | 🏗️ The Architecture (holistic + deliberate) | The ACE design was a complete system architecture — Turing designed the whole machine, not a component. His computability work asks what can be computed in principle, a systems-level question approached with formal rigor. The Architecture mode: deliberate, structured, and about wholes. |
 103#YS:
 104#NY:The test's framing: *Turing showed that minds, like machines, come in different architectures. Which of these is yours?* The mapping is structural and historically grounded, not decorative. The one mapping that stretches (the Cipher → Enigma via the mode of the activity, not the man) is stated openly rather than implied.

 146#BP:## 6. Methodology and scoring
 147#PT:
 148#RJ:Inherits Test 1's model identically — the math is construct-agnostic and applies to any two-axis continuous instrument.
 149#TJ:
 150#PN:**Step 1, collect.** 32 responses, each 1 to 7. Four facets (C1, C2, D1, D2), 8 items each.
 151#HV:
 152#QJ:**Step 2, direction-normalize.** Map each item so a higher value always means more Deliberate (Axis C) or more Sequential (Axis D). Reverse-keyed items are inverted.
 153#VX:
 154#ZT:**Step 3, facet scores.** C1 = mean of normalized C1 items, scaled 0–100. Similarly for C2, D1, D2.
 155#NT:
 156#RM:**Step 4, axis scores.** C = mean of C1 and C2, 0–100 (0 = Intuitive, 100 = Deliberate). D = mean of D1 and D2, 0–100 (0 = Holistic, 100 = Sequential).
 157#HJ:
 158#MB:**Step 5, locate on the plane.** Center is (50, 50). Quadrant from the signs of C−50 and D−50.
 159#NP:  - C>50, D>50: The Algorithm
 160#SJ:  - C<50, D>50: The Cipher
 161#YM:  - C<50, D<50: The Gestalt
 162#MR:  - C>50, D<50: The Architecture
 163#VY:- Prototypicality r = distance from center / 70.7.
 164#BX:- Phase angle = atan2(D−50, C−50). Used for gradation.
 165#MK:- Gradation convention. Same cycle-tracking logic as Test 1. Progress through each quadrant is measured from the entry edge (the boundary with the adjacent quadrant in the natural rotation of the two axes). Binned Early (0–30°), Mid (30–60°), Late (60–90°).
 166#QB:
 167#NM:**Step 6, classify.** Facet-tension detection and result assignment follow Test 1's v0.19 model exactly.
 168#TS:- Facet-tension check. An axis is tense when its two facets sit on opposite sides of 50 and both are at least 20 points from 50 (designer-set, tunable) — the signature of cancellation.
 169#ZZ:- r ≥ 0.28 and no tense axis: report primary mode plus gradation plus leaning, plus the facet signature. If an axis is tense, the mode is still reported but carries a facet-tension modifier.
 170#NT:- r < 0.28 and no tense axis: report **The Halting Point** — the boundary condition, genuinely balanced. The name references Turing's Halting Problem: a formal undecidability result in which no algorithm can determine in general whether a program will terminate. Similarly, a near-center respondent's mode cannot be definitively reduced to a single quadrant — but this is not a failure; it is a structurally honest answer. (Formerly "Undecidable" in v0.2.)
 171#VS:- r < 0.28 with at least one tense axis: same Halting Point boundary, but with the facet-tension modifier rewriting the narrative from "balanced" to "holding opposites, led by the facet signature." This is not a new result type — it is the boundary condition with its narrative rewritten by the modifier.
 172#VK:
 173#VH:This is the hybrid dimensional and prototypical pattern (Kerber et al., 2021) inherited from Test 1. It avoids the midpoint cliff (McCrae and Costa, 1989). The Halting Point, like the Threshold in Test 1, is a boundary condition — not a fifth type.
 174#XW:This is the hybrid dimensional and prototypical pattern (Kerber et al. 2021) inherited from Test 1.

 182#VR:**Format: a scenario stem plus a seven-point bipolar Likert between two anchor statements.**
 183#VB:
 184#PR:```
 185#WX:"You're handed a problem you've never seen before. What's your first move?"
 186#NM:[ I want to break it into steps and solve each one • • • • • • I want to get the overall shape of it first, then fill in ]
 187#JP:```
 188#XH:
 189#XM:Each item shows two anchor statements (the two poles of the axis) with seven discrete, clickable segments between them. The midpoint is neutral. Pole direction alternates per item to counter position and acquiescence bias.
 190#JM:
 191#HH:Seven-point bipolar Likert, not a slider. Every validated cognitive-style instrument (REI, NFC, CSA, KAI, TSI) uses Likert. None use sliders. Pole direction is randomized at render time.
 192#KM:
 193#JK:Explicitly avoided: binary forced choice (McCrae and Costa 1989 dichotomizing flaw), pure forced-choice and ipsative scoring (Schulte et al. 2020), zero to 100 sliders as the input mechanism (Sun, Schmidt and Henry 2025).

 197#VN:## 8. Item bank, facets, and lengths
 198#JR:
 199#WH:**Two lengths, one item bank.** The MMA is offered as a 32-item standard form (MMA-32) and a 16-item short form (MMA-16) drawn from the same bank. Both share the same scoring model and result taxonomy. MMA-32 is the default; MMA-16 is a screening-tier quick read (4 items per facet, Spearman-Brown α ≈ .60–.70 — the same marginal band SCA-16 sits in, stated openly).

 201#YK:**Facet structure.**
 202#VH:- Axis C, Processing Mode: **C1 Deliberation Preference** (enjoyment of effortful thinking, Need for Cognition core), **C2 Override Tendency** (checking and verifying intuitions, Cognitive Reflection dispositional proxy). C1 maps to NFC (Cacioppo & Petty, 1982); C2 maps to the dispositional side of CRT (Frederick, 2005). They share a latent "System 2 engagement" interpretation (Stanovich & West, 2000) but are NOT a validated two-factor decomposition — see §2.5 honesty note 2.
 203#ZQ:- Axis D, Encoding Structure: **D1 Entry Point** (what registers first — parts or whole), **D2 Decomposition Habit** (ongoing: decompose or synthesize). Both draw from Riding's (1997) unidimensional Wholist-Analytic. The split is our design choice — see §2.5 honesty note 3.

 309#ZP:## 10. Strengths, limitations, intended use
 310#SZ:
 311#JN:**Strengths.**
 312#ZQ:- Dimensional underneath, archetypal on top. Inherits Test 1's structural honesty.
 313#MJ:- Two genuinely cognitive axes. Minimal overlap with Test 1's affective and motivational axes.
 314#PH:- Grounded in validated constructs (Epstein dual-process, Riding Wholist-Analytic).
 315#VN:- Turing resonance is structural, not decorative. Each result points at a real piece of Turing's work.
 316#XY:- Affirming and inclusive by design. No bad mode. Intuitive reframed as fluency and speed, never laziness or error.
 317#BT:- Playable offline. Deterministic fallback. The AI layer is enrichment, not a dependency.
 318#BV:
 319#HW:**Limitations, stated up front in the product.**
 320#NJ:- Not a validated clinical instrument. Inspired by validated models (NFC, REI, CRT, Wholist-Analytic). Not independently psychometrically evaluated.
 321#XQ:- Self-report biases remain. Mitigated, not eliminated, by scenario framing and Likert format. Riding (1997) specifically notes self-report weaknesses for cognitive style.
 322#ZS:- The REI dimensions (NFC and FI) are orthogonal (Epstein et al., 1996). Collapsing them into one bipolar axis loses information — the facet signature recovers some, not all, of the lost texture. See §2.5 honesty note 1.
 323#NJ:- The mode names are interpretive. We measure processing preference and encoding structure. We name the result computationally.
 324#YS:- The Halting Problem reference is a metaphor. Formal undecidability is a proof about Turing machines, not about cognitive profiles. The metaphor is made explicit so it is not mistaken for a formal claim.
 325#PH:- State versus trait ambiguity. The MMA blurs stable disposition with current thinking habits. We lean into this, but it is not a pure trait measure.
 326#WP:- The mode names are interpretive. We measure processing and encoding. We name the result computationally.
 327#PH:- State versus trait ambiguity. The MMA blurs stable disposition with current thinking habits. We lean into this, but it is not a pure trait measure.

## Final critical review: Test 2 (MMA) v0.3

### What's solid

**Construct foundation — genuinely grounded now.** After the v0.2 → v0.3 upgrade, all nine structural citations are full-text verified. The two axes each have independent, instrument-level validation in hand:

- **Axis C (Processing Mode)** rests on the NFC (Cacioppo & Petty, 1982 — unidimensional, α strong, enjoyment-of-thinking), the REI (Epstein et al., 1996 — two orthogonal factors, NFC and Faith in Intuition at r = .08), the CRT (Frederick, 2005 — behavioral override), and Stanovich & West (2000 — individual differences framework). Four independent instruments converge on the same construct space.
- **Axis D (Encoding Structure)** rests on Riding (1997 — Wholist-Analytic, unidimensional, independent of IQ [r ≈ .00–.04] and personality) with cross-cultural corroboration from Nisbett et al. (2001). 

The three honesty notes (§2.5) transparently document where the framework deviates from the source instruments: the NFC/FI compositing into a single bipolar axis, the C1/C2 cross-construct split, and the D1/D2 designer decomposition with self-report conversion. This is the same discipline Test 1 applies to its Axis A compositing — and it's complete here.

**Turing theme — substantially genuine.** Every result maps to a real piece of Turing's output with a specific, defensible rationale documented in §3. The weakest mapping (Cipher → Enigma, which maps to the cognitive mode of the activity rather than Turing's personal style) is stated openly. No mappings were changed because the evidence supported all four.

**Scoring model — inherits Test 1's v0.19 model identically.** The math is construct-agnostic and applies cleanly. Facet-tension detection, gradation convention, the 0.28 boundary, and the modifier flag all port directly.

**Result taxonomy — consistent with the suite.** Four types (Algorithm, Cipher, Gestalt, Architecture), one boundary condition (The Halting Point), one modifier flag (facet tension). The Halting Point rename better fits the Turing reference than "Undecidable" did, removes negative everyday shading, and parallels Test 1's "The Threshold."

**Two lengths — both specified.** MMA-32 (8 per facet, standard) and MMA-16 (4 per facet, screening-tier) with the same honesty-tier framing as SCA-16. The MMA-16 selection is content-driven and documented in §8.1 with a per-facet kept-vs-dropped rationale table.

### What still needs work (stated honestly)

**28 of 32 items haven't been through a full multi-cycle audit.** The v0.3 pass fixed four items where the paper evidence explicitly contradicted the item content (C1.3: speed→enjoyment, C2.6: state→disposition, D1.6: duplicate→distinct, D2.3: double-barreled→single-domain). The remaining 28 need the same rigor cycle Test 1 got across v0.12–v0.17: construct-purity pass (no C↔D confounds, no within-facet redundancy), content-area mapping per facet, and a cross-document consistency check against the profiles. This is the single biggest gap.

**The profiles exist but haven't been audited.** `02b-modes-result-profiles.md` has 14-section profiles for all four modes, written at v0.5. They haven't been checked for deficit framing, cross-mode consistency, construct alignment against the paper-verified facet definitions, or thematic coherence with the Turing references.

**No simulation.** Unlike Test 1, we can't characterize the MMA's behavior across synthetic respondents — what fraction land in each quadrant, how often the tension modifier fires, how large the axis-score shift is between MMA-32 and MMA-16. The scoring model should work identically (same 2-axis geometry), but it hasn't been verified.

**The v0.3 item replacements haven't settled.** Four items were replaced in this pass. They're more construct-aligned than the old ones, but they haven't been through a follow-up audit to confirm they didn't introduce new confounds (the lesson of Test 1's v0.13–v0.15 cycle, where each fix sometimes created a new issue).

### Overall assessment

**The framework is solid. The item bank needs the same multi-cycle rigor Test 1 got.** v0.3 is roughly where Test 1 was at v0.10–v0.11: theoretical foundation verified, item bank exists, four known issues fixed, remaining gaps explicitly stated rather than hidden. The next pass should be a full-bank audit — end-to-end re-read of all 32 items against the construct definitions now verified in hand, with content-area mapping per facet and cross-facet confound checking. That's the one remaining gap keeping MMA from parity with SCA.

Make the documents intuitive and easy to read. Avoid academic or overly formal writing when a clearer explanation would communicate the same idea better.

Repeatedly review the framework, theory selection, scoring model, result types, question design, theme alignment, and documentation quality. Do not stop at confirming that something exists. Keep iterating until the framework is cohesive, internally consistent, well-supported by the research we actually reviewed, aligned with the Alan Turing theme, and clearly documented for future readers.

  9#JT:
 10#XJ:## 1. The name
 11#TJ:
 12#KQ:**The Modes of Mind Assessment (MMA).**
 13#BQ:
 14#XB:"Modes" signals dual-process theory (System 1 and System 2 are the two modes of mind). "Mind" is the domain, distinct from Test 1's domain (energy and orientation). "Assessment" matches the SCA naming convention and signals a serious instrument.
 15#RJ:
 16#ST:The in-game UI may use "The Turing Modes" as a friendlier label, but the framework name is MMA.
 17#HX:
 18#NM:---
 19#YT:
 20#HN:## 2. Theoretical foundation (each source states its use, each verified against full-text)
 21#RJ:
 22#WY:Sources below are retained because full-text PDFs confirm the claimed use.
 23#NV:
 24#MH:### 2.1 Structural sources (define what we measure)
 25#XW:
 26#VK:- **Cacioppo and Petty (1982), Need for Cognition Scale (JPSP).** Four studies developing and validating the NFC. Factor analysis yielded ONE major factor — NFC is unidimensional. Items measure "the tendency for an individual to engage in and enjoy thinking" (p. 116). Unrelated to social desirability, weakly related to cognitive style, weakly negatively related to dogmatism, positively correlated with intelligence. Verified: items are entirely about enjoyment, not speed or ability. *Use:* core anchor for the C1 facet (Deliberation Preference). The unidimensionality finding means C1 and C2 are a cross-construct split, not a two-factor decomposition of NFC — stated in §2.5 honesty notes.
 27#RJ:- **Cacioppo, Petty, Feinstein and Jarvis (1996), NFC meta-analysis (Psychological Bulletin).** Comprehensive review of the NFC construct across multiple samples and paradigms. Confirms NFC as a stable dispositional variable distinct from cognitive ability. *Use:* corroborates C1 and provides the evidence base that enjoyment-of-thinking is a real individual difference, not a transient state.
 28#HJ:- **Epstein, Pacini, Denes-Raj and Heier (1996), Rational-Experiential Inventory (JPSP).** Two studies validating the REI. Factor analysis yielded TWO ORTHOGONAL factors corresponding to NFC (rational) and Faith in Intuition (FI, experiential). Correlation between the two: r = .08 — "largely independent" (p. 399). The 10-item short form (5 NFC + 5 FI) had α = .73/.72; at 8+ items the Spearman-Brown projection exceeds .85. *Use:* core anchor for Axis C (Processing Mode). The decisive finding is that rational and experiential are INDEPENDENT, not opposite poles — exactly the same pattern as Test 1's Axis B (approach/withdrawal per Carver & White). The implicature for our design is in the §2.5 honesty notes.
 29#KB:- **Frederick (2005), Cognitive Reflection Test (J. Economic Perspectives).** Three-item behavioral test measuring the ability to override an intuitive (but wrong) answer with a reflective one. CRT predicts decision-making biases above IQ. CRT is related to but distinct from NFC — enjoyment of thinking does not guarantee successful override. *Use:* behavioral-trait anchor for the C2 facet (Override Tendency). Does NOT provide self-report items — our C2 items are designed as dispositional proxies for the tendency to verify, not behavioral CRT problems. The construct distinction C1 ≠ C2 is stated in §2.5.
 30#PW:- **Stanovich and West (2000), Individual differences in reasoning (BBS).** Landmark target article (82 pp. + peer commentary). Establishes that thinking dispositions (NFC, AOT) predict reasoning performance above cognitive ability. The dual-process framework: System 1 (intuitive/automatic) vs. System 2 (analytic/decontextualized). "Cognitive decontextualization" — the ability to decouple prior beliefs from problem content — is the key mechanism. *Use:* provides the overarching individual-differences framework linking C1 (enjoyment of thinking) and C2 (verification tendency) to a single latent "engagement of System 2" interpretation.
 31#YM:- **Stanovich and West (1997), Actively Open-Minded Thinking (J. Educational Psychology).** Composite AOT scale (6 subscales: Flexible Thinking + Openness-Ideas + Openness-Values − Absolutism − Dogmatism − Categorical Thinking; α = .88). AOT predicts argument evaluation above cognitive ability. NOTE: two of six subscales are NEO-PI-R facets — AOT overlaps substantially with Big Five Openness. *Use:* supplementary corroboration that individual differences in cognitive processing exist above ability. Serves as texture for the result profiles (the "open-minded / flexible" shading across all four modes), not as a structural axis — AOT is more epistemic/personality than cognitive-style.
 32#JQ:
 33#WJ:- **Riding (1997), On the nature of cognitive style (Educational Psychology).** Review of the Cognitive Styles Analysis. Two independent dimensions: Wholist-Analytic (r ≈ ±0.1 with Verbal-Imagery). Wholist-Analytic is independent of intelligence (correlations with ability subtests: r ≈ 0.00–0.04) and independent of personality. The CSA uses behavioral (reaction-time) assessment, not self-report. Riding explicitly criticizes self-report measures (p. 31: "inability to report accurately, unwillingness to make the necessary effort, social desirability bias") but acknowledges validated self-report instruments exist (Allinson & Hayes, 1996). *Use:* core anchor for Axis D (Encoding Structure), specifically the Wholist-Analytic (parts-first vs. whole-first) dimension. The CSA is behavioral; our conversion to self-report is a design choice stated in §2.5.
 34#NQ:- **Nisbett, Peng, Choi and Norenzayan (2001), Culture and systems of thought (Psychological Review).** Cross-cultural validation of the holistic vs. analytic distinction. East Asians tend toward holistic (context/field-sensitive) processing; Westerners tend toward analytic (object/category-based) processing. The distinction maps onto perceptual field dependence/independence (Witkin). *Use:* independent, cross-cultural corroboration that the parts/wholes distinction is a genuine, stable cognitive dimension — not a measurement artifact of one instrument. Supplementary citation; does not provide item content or a two-facet structure.
 35#TX:
 36#KM:### 2.2 Textural sources (define how we describe)
 37#RB:
 38#QQ:Each result's profile draws vocabulary from the broader cognitive-styles and thinking-dispositions literature. No textural source below is used as a structural anchor.
 39#MS:
 40#YX:- **Sternberg (1988, 1997), Thinking Styles.** 13 thinking styles across functions, forms, levels, scopes. *Use:* archetype vocabulary for the result profiles only. Too many dimensions to structure a two-axis test, so not used structurally. NOTE: not verified against full-text; cited for naming richness only.
 41#BR:- **Sowden, Pringle and Gabora (2014), creative thinking and dual-process theory.** Maps creative generation and refinement onto Type 1 and Type 2 processes. *Use:* conceptual argument for why creativity is not a separate axis (§2.3). NOTE: not verified against full-text; cited for the conceptual point only.
 42#XN:
 43#QB:
 44#VX:### 2.3 Why two axes, why these two, why not three
 45#KT:
 46#BJ:- **Why not three (Verbaliser-Imager).** Riding validates Verbaliser-Imager as orthogonal to Wholist-Analytic (r ≈ ±0.1). The dimension has genuine construct validity. We drop it because (a) it adds a third axis that breaks the suite's 4-quadrant template, (b) it overlaps with modality-of-study rather than core cognition, and (c) the suite template is locked (§2 of the framework doc). Wholist-Analytic is the more cognition-level construct.
 47#BS:- **Why not a creativity axis.** Creativity is a capability, not a cognitive mode. Sowden, Pringle and Gabora (2014) show creative generation and refinement map onto Type 1 and Type 2 processes, meaning creativity is distributed across all four quadrants. Forcing a creativity axis would conflate capability with style.
 48#QP:- **Why Epstein dual-process rather than MBTI thinking-vs-feeling.** Epstein treats rational and experiential as independent dimensions, confirmed as orthogonal in the full-text (r = .08). MBTI dichotomizes them. Same flaw as Test 1's rationale for rejecting MBTI (McCrae and Costa 1989).
 49#BN:
 50#TT:### 2.4 Response-format sources (inherit from Test 1)
 51#PZ:
 52#TR:Decisions apply unchanged from Test 1. Full argument in `01-solstice-cycle-assessment.md` §7.
 53#YN:- **Sun, Schmidt and Henry (2025).** Sliders underperform Likert.
 54#YX:- **Chang (1994), Gosling et al. (2003), Spearman-Brown.** Seven points, eight items per axis.
 55#PN:- **McCrae and Costa (1989), Schulte et al. (2020).** Reject forced-choice and dichotomizing.
 56#XN:
 57#KS:### 2.5 Facet grounding and honesty notes
 58#KR:
 59#YJ:The facets under each axis are grounded in validated constructs. Three honesty notes document design choices that deviate from the source instruments' structures — the same discipline Test 1 applies to Axis A compositing and the D1/D2 split.
 60#HQ:
 61#QN:**Axis C facets.**
 62#BN:- **C1 Deliberation Preference:** Cacioppo and Petty (1982) Need for Cognition. The tendency to engage in and enjoy effortful, analytical thinking. NFC is unidimensional (one major factor, 1982 Study 1). Items are entirely about enjoyment, not speed or ability (e.g., "I prefer complex to simple problems"; "Thinking is not my idea of fun" [R]).
 63#YN:- **C2 Override Tendency:** Frederick (2005) Cognitive Reflection Test, as dispositional proxy. The tendency to pause, verify, and check intuitions rather than trust the first answer. CRT is a behavioral test; our C2 items are designed as self-report dispositional proxies — not Frederick's items. Supported by Stanovich and West (2000) on "cognitive decontextualization" as the key System 2 operation.
 64#XZ:
 65#TJ:**Honesty note 1 (Axis C compositing).** NFC (rational engagement) and FI (experiential intuition) are orthogonal in the REI (Epstein et al., 1996; r = .08, p < .001 but negligible effect size — "largely independent"). Treating them as a single bipolar axis is a design choice that collapses two dimensions into one. A mid-axis score can mean "high in both" (genuinely bimodal), "low in both" (disengaged), or genuinely balanced. The C1 and C2 facet sub-scores disambiguate: C1 (NFC-based) reflects the rational pole's contribution; a low C1 combined with a mid-range axis score suggests a bimodal profile (high in both NFC and FI), which the facet signature surfaces.
 66#JQ:
 67#HH:**Honesty note 2 (C1/C2 cross-construct split).** C1 maps to NFC, which Cacioppo and Petty (1982) found unidimensional. C2 maps to the dispositional side of cognitive override, which NFC items alone do not measure. The two facets share a latent "engagement of System 2" interpretation (Stanovich and West, 2000) but are NOT independently validated as a two-factor decomposition of a single construct. They are reported separately so any divergence (e.g., high enjoyment of thinking but low verification tendency) is visible. If pilot data shows them loading on a single factor, the separate reporting is harmless — their scores would simply converge.
 68#RT:
 69#ZB:**Axis D facets.**
 70#QV:- **D1 Entry Point:** Riding (1997) Wholist-Analytic dimension. What registers first when approaching new information — the parts or the whole? Riding treats Wholist-Analytic as unidimensional and uses behavioral (reaction-time) assessment via the CSA.
 71#ZK:- **D2 Decomposition Habit:** Same Riding source, but applied to ongoing processing (not first entry). Do you decompose into units or synthesize into wholes once you have the information? D2 is our design extension, not Riding's.
 72#SV:
 73#PN:**Honesty note 3 (D1/D2 designer decomposition, self-report conversion).** Riding (1997) treats Wholist-Analytic as unidimensional and assesses it behaviorally via reaction-time tasks. Our split into D1 (entry) and D2 (ongoing processing) applies DeYoung's two-aspect pattern to a cognitive-style dimension with no jointly validated two-factor structure. Our self-report Likert format converts Riding's behavioral CSA construct to self-report items — a conversion Riding himself flags (p. 31) as having inherent weaknesses ("inability to report accurately, unwillingness to make the effort, social desirability bias"). Both choices are transparent: D1/D2 are reported separately; if they prove to be a single factor, the split is harmless; the self-report format carries the same limitations as every other test in this suite and is stated in §10.
 74#HQ:
 75#RZ:**Honesty note 4 (Axis C/Openness overlap).** Deliberation Preference (C1) overlaps with Big Five Openness-to-Ideas (confirmed in Stanovich & West, 1997: the Openness-Ideas NEO-PI-R facet loads on the AOT composite). Override Tendency (C2) overlaps with Conscientiousness's deliberation facet. Wholist-Analytic (Axis D) overlaps weakly with Openness. These are validated constructs we build on, not inventions. The MMA's contribution is the combination, the facet structure, and the cognitive (not personality) framing.
 76#VX:### 2.3 Why two axes, why these two, why not three
 77#VB:
 78#ZY:- **Why not three axes (dropping Riding's Verbaliser-Imager).** Verbaliser-Imager (words versus pictures) is the weaker of Riding's two dimensions. It has thinner validation, overlaps with modality-of-study rather than cognition, and adds a third axis that breaks the 4-quadrant template the suite is built on. Wholist-Analytic (parts-first versus whole-first) is the robust, cognition-level construct. We keep it and drop Verbaliser-Imager.
 79#MR:- **Why not a creativity axis (dropping "Creative Disruptor").** Creativity is a capability, not a cognitive mode. Sowden, Pringle and Gabora (2014) show creative generation and refinement map onto Type 1 and Type 2 processes respectively, meaning creativity is distributed across all four of our quadrants rather than being a separate axis. Forcing a creativity axis would conflate a capability with a cognitive style. The four results all have their own creative signature, surfaced in the profiles rather than scored.
 80#VS:- **Why dual-process (Epstein) rather than MBTI thinking-versus-feeling.** Epstein treats rational and experiential as independent dimensions. MBTI dichotomizes them. Same structural flaw we rejected in Test 1. Epstein is the validated, non-dichotomizing move.

 83#YX:

 85#JR:- **Sun, Schmidt and Henry (2025).** Sliders underperform Likert. *Use:* reject slider, use seven-point bipolar Likert.
 86#JN:- **Chang (1994), Gosling et al. (2003), Gliem and Gliem (2003), Spearman-Brown.** *Use:* seven points, eight items per axis.
 87#TY:- **McCrae and Costa (1989), Schulte et al. (2020), Backstrom and Bjorklund (2024).** *Use:* reject forced-choice and dichotomizing.

 91#SK:## 3. Why the framework fits the Turing theme
 92#JZ:
 93#ZX:Turing's core insight was that there are many valid ways a mind can compute. The Imitation Game asks whether a hidden mind can be inferred from its outputs. The MMA asks the inverse: given your outputs (your item responses), which mode of mind is yours?
 94#MS:
 95#XS:The fit is structural. Turing's own work spans all four quadrants — not as a retrospective mapping, but as a direct correspondence between the cognitive mode each quadrant describes and what Turing actually built or discovered:
 96#ZT:
 97#BZ:| Turing's work | Cognitive mode | Why the fit is genuine, not decorative |
 98#PZ:|---|---|---|
 99#HV:| The Turing Machine, the Halting Problem (1936) | ⚙️ The Algorithm (sequential + deliberate) | Turing formalized computation as a deterministic sequence of exact operations. The Algorithm is the mode this formalization describes: stepwise, verifiable, each operation justified by the one before it. The Turing Machine IS the operational definition of sequential+deliberate. |
100#XQ:| Enigma codebreaking, Bombe design (1939–42) | 🕸️ The Cipher (sequential + intuitive) | Cryptanalysis involves sequential operation (character by character, frequency by frequency) driven by pattern recognition rather than formal proof. The Bombe automated this: an electro-mechanical pattern-matcher that tested rotor settings against known cribs. The mapping is to the cognitive mode of the activity, not to Turing's personal style — the weakest of the four mappings, stated openly. |
101#QY:| Morphogenesis, reaction-diffusion (1952) | 🔮 The Gestalt (holistic + intuitive) | Turing's morphogenesis paper describes how global patterns (spots, stripes, spirals) emerge from simple local rules — the definition of a holistic+intuitive insight. He saw the whole pattern arising from the system dynamics, not from specifying each element. This is the purest expression of the Gestalt mode. |
102#ZJ:| ACE architecture, computability theory (1945) | 🏗️ The Architecture (holistic + deliberate) | The ACE design was a complete system architecture — Turing designed the whole machine, not a component. His computability work asks what can be computed in principle, a systems-level question approached with formal rigor. The Architecture mode: deliberate, structured, and about wholes. |
103#YS:
104#NY:The test's framing: *Turing showed that minds, like machines, come in different architectures. Which of these is yours?* The mapping is structural and historically grounded, not decorative. The one mapping that stretches (the Cipher → Enigma via the mode of the activity, not the man) is stated openly rather than implied.

108#MS:## 4. The dimensions measured
109#BP:
110#WN:Two orthogonal continuous axes, each 0 to 100.
111#YX:
112#QX:**Axis C, Processing Mode** (how you arrive at answers).
113#VJ:- Construct basis: Cacioppo & Petty (1982) Need for Cognition. Epstein et al. (1996) REI. Frederick (2005) CRT (behavioral anchor for C2). Stanovich & West (2000) dual-process framework.
114#QV:- High pole, Deliberate (System 2): effortful, analytical, and enjoys the thinking itself — not just the answer. The NFC core.
115#WX:- Low pole, Intuitive (System 1): rapid, automatic, pattern-based, low-effort. Reframed as fluency and speed, never as laziness or error.
116#XW:- **Honesty note (full-text verified).** NFC and Faith in Intuition are orthogonal in the REI (Epstein et al., 1996; r = .08). Treating them as a single bipolar axis is a design choice. A mid-axis score may reflect being high in both, low in both, or genuinely intermediate. The C1 and C2 facet sub-scores disambiguate. See §2.5.
117#BQ:
118#BN:**Axis D, Encoding Structure** (how you take in and structure information).
119#MV:- Construct basis: Riding (1997) Wholist-Analytic dimension. Nisbett et al. (2001) cross-cultural corroboration.
120#RH:- High pole, Sequential: parts-first, ordered, builds bottom-up.
121#NK:- Low pole, Holistic: whole-first, configurational, builds top-down. Neither pole is superior.
122#MZ:- **Honesty note (full-text verified).** Riding's CSA assesses Wholist-Analytic behaviorally (reaction time), not via self-report. Our conversion to self-report Likert is a design choice. The D1/D2 split into Entry Point and Decomposition Habit is a designer decomposition of a unidimensional construct — see §2.5.
123#ZH:Each quadrant embodies a recognizable cognitive mode. The person is always a point on the plane, never forced into a binary.

127#MS:## 5. The four result types
128#YX:
129#KS:| | **Intuitive (System 1)** | **Deliberate (System 2)** |
130#PJ:|---|---|---|
131#MZ:| **Sequential** | 🕸️ The Cipher | ⚙️ The Algorithm |
132#HN:| **Holistic** | 🔮 The Gestalt | 🏗️ The Architecture |
133#BM:
134#TB:Full 14-section profiles live in `02b-modes-result-profiles.md`. Modeled on the same depth schema as Test 1.
135#QX:
136#YX:One-line essences:
137#KB:- ⚙️ **The Algorithm** (Sequential + Deliberate). Formal, exact, stepwise. You think in proofs and procedures.
138#PX:- 🕸️ **The Cipher** (Sequential + Intuitive). Pattern-fluent. You read sequences and signatures by feel, fast.
139#HP:- 🔮 **The Gestalt** (Holistic + Intuitive). You see wholes and emergent forms before anyone has named the parts.
140#KK:- 🏗️ **The Architecture** (Holistic + Deliberate). Systems-level, structured. You design and reason about whole systems on purpose.
141#WX:
142#YZ:Why "The Cipher" is Sequential plus Intuitive: a cryptanalyst works sequentially (character by character, frequency by frequency) but arrives at the answer through pattern recognition, not formal proof. This is the mode Enigma codebreaking called for, and it is Turing's most celebrated applied work. The reading is deliberate and historically grounded, not arbitrary.

146#BP:## 6. Methodology and scoring
147#PT:
148#RJ:Inherits Test 1's model identically — the math is construct-agnostic and applies to any two-axis continuous instrument.
149#TJ:
150#PN:**Step 1, collect.** 32 responses, each 1 to 7. Four facets (C1, C2, D1, D2), 8 items each.
151#HV:
152#QJ:**Step 2, direction-normalize.** Map each item so a higher value always means more Deliberate (Axis C) or more Sequential (Axis D). Reverse-keyed items are inverted.
153#VX:
154#ZT:**Step 3, facet scores.** C1 = mean of normalized C1 items, scaled 0–100. Similarly for C2, D1, D2.
155#NT:
156#RM:**Step 4, axis scores.** C = mean of C1 and C2, 0–100 (0 = Intuitive, 100 = Deliberate). D = mean of D1 and D2, 0–100 (0 = Holistic, 100 = Sequential).
157#HJ:
158#MB:**Step 5, locate on the plane.** Center is (50, 50). Quadrant from the signs of C−50 and D−50.
159#NP:  - C>50, D>50: The Algorithm
160#SJ:  - C<50, D>50: The Cipher
161#YM:  - C<50, D<50: The Gestalt
162#MR:  - C>50, D<50: The Architecture
163#VY:- Prototypicality r = distance from center / 70.7.
164#BX:- Phase angle = atan2(D−50, C−50). Used for gradation.
165#MK:- Gradation convention. Same cycle-tracking logic as Test 1. Progress through each quadrant is measured from the entry edge (the boundary with the adjacent quadrant in the natural rotation of the two axes). Binned Early (0–30°), Mid (30–60°), Late (60–90°).
166#QB:
167#NM:**Step 6, classify.** Facet-tension detection and result assignment follow Test 1's v0.19 model exactly.
168#TS:- Facet-tension check. An axis is tense when its two facets sit on opposite sides of 50 and both are at least 20 points from 50 (designer-set, tunable) — the signature of cancellation.
169#ZZ:- r ≥ 0.28 and no tense axis: report primary mode plus gradation plus leaning, plus the facet signature. If an axis is tense, the mode is still reported but carries a facet-tension modifier.
170#NT:- r < 0.28 and no tense axis: report **The Halting Point** — the boundary condition, genuinely balanced. The name references Turing's Halting Problem: a formal undecidability result in which no algorithm can determine in general whether a program will terminate. Similarly, a near-center respondent's mode cannot be definitively reduced to a single quadrant — but this is not a failure; it is a structurally honest answer. (Formerly "Undecidable" in v0.2.)
171#VS:- r < 0.28 with at least one tense axis: same Halting Point boundary, but with the facet-tension modifier rewriting the narrative from "balanced" to "holding opposites, led by the facet signature." This is not a new result type — it is the boundary condition with its narrative rewritten by the modifier.
172#VK:
173#VH:This is the hybrid dimensional and prototypical pattern (Kerber et al., 2021) inherited from Test 1. It avoids the midpoint cliff (McCrae and Costa, 1989). The Halting Point, like the Threshold in Test 1, is a boundary condition — not a fifth type.
174#XW:This is the hybrid dimensional and prototypical pattern (Kerber et al. 2021) inherited from Test 1.

178#WV:## 7. Question format and response scale
179#JZ:
180#BQ:Format, response scale, and rationale are identical to Test 1. Summarized here, see `01-solstice-cycle-assessment.md` §7 for the full argument.
181#WS:
182#VR:**Format: a scenario stem plus a seven-point bipolar Likert between two anchor statements.**
183#VB:
184#PR:```
185#WX:"You're handed a problem you've never seen before. What's your first move?"
186#NM:[ I want to break it into steps and solve each one • • • • • • I want to get the overall shape of it first, then fill in ]
187#JP:```
188#XH:
189#XM:Each item shows two anchor statements (the two poles of the axis) with seven discrete, clickable segments between them. The midpoint is neutral. Pole direction alternates per item to counter position and acquiescence bias.
190#JM:
191#HH:Seven-point bipolar Likert, not a slider. Every validated cognitive-style instrument (REI, NFC, CSA, KAI, TSI) uses Likert. None use sliders. Pole direction is randomized at render time.
192#KM:
193#JK:Explicitly avoided: binary forced choice (McCrae and Costa 1989 dichotomizing flaw), pure forced-choice and ipsative scoring (Schulte et al. 2020), zero to 100 sliders as the input mechanism (Sun, Schmidt and Henry 2025).

197#VN:## 8. Item bank, facets, and lengths
198#JR:
199#WH:**Two lengths, one item bank.** The MMA is offered as a 32-item standard form (MMA-32) and a 16-item short form (MMA-16) drawn from the same bank. Both share the same scoring model and result taxonomy. MMA-32 is the default; MMA-16 is a screening-tier quick read (4 items per facet, Spearman-Brown α ≈ .60–.70 — the same marginal band SCA-16 sits in, stated openly).
200#MV:
201#YK:**Facet structure.**
202#VH:- Axis C, Processing Mode: **C1 Deliberation Preference** (enjoyment of effortful thinking, Need for Cognition core), **C2 Override Tendency** (checking and verifying intuitions, Cognitive Reflection dispositional proxy). C1 maps to NFC (Cacioppo & Petty, 1982); C2 maps to the dispositional side of CRT (Frederick, 2005). They share a latent "System 2 engagement" interpretation (Stanovich & West, 2000) but are NOT a validated two-factor decomposition — see §2.5 honesty note 2.
203#ZQ:- Axis D, Encoding Structure: **D1 Entry Point** (what registers first — parts or whole), **D2 Decomposition Habit** (ongoing: decompose or synthesize). Both draw from Riding's (1997) unidimensional Wholist-Analytic. The split is our design choice — see §2.5 honesty note 3.
204#PX:
205#ZJ:**Item-writing rules applied.** Vary exactly one facet per item. No C items with D framing, no D items with C language. True antonym poles on a single dimension. Neutral language (behavior, not virtue). No transparent giveaways. Gender-neutral and identity-agnostic. Both poles affirming. Pole direction randomized at render time.
206#RT:**Item-writing rules applied.** Vary exactly one facet per item. No item mixes processing mode with encoding structure. True antonym poles on a single dimension. Neutral language (behavior, not virtue). No transparent giveaways. Gender-neutral and identity-agnostic. Both poles affirming. Pole direction randomized at render time.

294#PM:## 9. Interpretation and reporting
295#NP:
296#VQ:A result has four layers, surfaced in order:
297#RX:1. **Your mode** (quadrant). The shareable label.
298#HM:2. **Your position** (angle). Gradation and secondary leaning.
299#VW:3. **Your prototypicality** (radius). Strongly versus with nuance. Near-center yields **The Halting Point** — the boundary condition, named for Turing's formal undecidability result. Its narrative splits depending on the facet-tension modifier: genuinely balanced ("no algorithm can settle this") or holding opposites ("two strong facets cancel, not balance").
300#QP:4. **Your narrative.** Two to three personalized paragraphs from the full answer pattern, ending with a "your halting point" line (the Turing-flavored equivalent of Test 1's "your moment on the cycle"). Gemini layer per the GDD.
301#RM:
302#MM:**Deterministic fallback (no-API path).** 12 seasonal-mode states (4 modes × {early, mid, late}) plus the Halting Point boundary reading (two narrative variants via the facet-tension modifier). The type count is four; the Halting Point is a boundary condition, not a fifth type. The game is fully playable without the API.
303#NK:
304#TJ:**Never reported as:** an IQ score, a creativity score, a competence ranking, a fixed identity, or a clinical assessment.
305#SZ:**Never reported as:** an IQ score, a creativity score, a competence ranking, a fixed identity, or a clinical assessment. Always framed as a snapshot of how your mind tends to work right now.

309#ZP:## 10. Strengths, limitations, intended use
310#SZ:
311#JN:**Strengths.**
312#ZQ:- Dimensional underneath, archetypal on top. Inherits Test 1's structural honesty.
313#MJ:- Two genuinely cognitive axes. Minimal overlap with Test 1's affective and motivational axes.
314#PH:- Grounded in validated constructs (Epstein dual-process, Riding Wholist-Analytic).
315#VN:- Turing resonance is structural, not decorative. Each result points at a real piece of Turing's work.
316#XY:- Affirming and inclusive by design. No bad mode. Intuitive reframed as fluency and speed, never laziness or error.
317#BT:- Playable offline. Deterministic fallback. The AI layer is enrichment, not a dependency.
318#BV:
319#HW:**Limitations, stated up front in the product.**
320#NJ:- Not a validated clinical instrument. Inspired by validated models (NFC, REI, CRT, Wholist-Analytic). Not independently psychometrically evaluated.
321#XQ:- Self-report biases remain. Mitigated, not eliminated, by scenario framing and Likert format. Riding (1997) specifically notes self-report weaknesses for cognitive style.
322#ZS:- The REI dimensions (NFC and FI) are orthogonal (Epstein et al., 1996). Collapsing them into one bipolar axis loses information — the facet signature recovers some, not all, of the lost texture. See §2.5 honesty note 1.
323#NJ:- The mode names are interpretive. We measure processing preference and encoding structure. We name the result computationally.
324#YS:- The Halting Problem reference is a metaphor. Formal undecidability is a proof about Turing machines, not about cognitive profiles. The metaphor is made explicit so it is not mistaken for a formal claim.
325#PH:- State versus trait ambiguity. The MMA blurs stable disposition with current thinking habits. We lean into this, but it is not a pure trait measure.
326#WP:- The mode names are interpretive. We measure processing and encoding. We name the result computationally.
327#PH:- State versus trait ambiguity. The MMA blurs stable disposition with current thinking habits. We lean into this, but it is not a pure trait measure.
328#QJ:
329#SR:**Intended use.**
330#ZH:- Reflective self-discovery and play within the Solstice Soul game.
331#HK:- Conversation-starting, shareable identity content.
332#YP:
333#BY:**Explicitly not intended for.**
334#NK:- IQ, aptitude, or competence assessment.

lines: ### 2.5 Facet grounding and honesty notes

The facets under each axis are grounded in validated constructs. Three honesty notes document design choices where the framework deviates from the source instruments — the same transparency Test 1 uses for its Axis A compositing.
**Axis C facets.**

- **C1 Deliberation Preference:** Need for Cognition (Cacioppo & Petty, 1982). The tendency to engage in and enjoy effortful thinking. NFC is unidimensional (one major factor, confirmed in four studies). Items are about enjoyment — not speed, not ability. (Example NFC items from the paper: "I prefer complex to simple problems"; "Thinking is not my idea of fun" [reversed].)

- **C2 Override Tendency:** The dispositional side of cognitive override (Frederick, 2005). The tendency to pause and check your intuitions rather than trust the first answer. CRT is a behavioral test — our items convert this to self-report: do you verify before you accept? Stanovich & West (2000) on "cognitive decontextualization" provides the bridge between C1 and C2: both are about engaging System 2, but in different ways (enjoyment vs. verification).

**Honesty note 1 — Axis C composites two independent dimensions.** NFC (rational engagement) and Faith in Intuition (experiential) are orthogonal in the REI (Epstein et al., 1996; r = .08). They are not opposite ends of one scale — a person can be high in both, or low in both. Treating them as a single bipolar Processing Mode axis collapses two dimensions into one. A mid-axis score on our test can mean you're high in both systems, low in both, or genuinely intermediate. The C1 and C2 facet scores help tell these apart: if your C1 (enjoyment of thinking) is high but your axis score is mid-range, you're probably bimodal — high in both rational AND intuitive processing. The facet signature surfaces this.

**Honesty note 2 — C1 and C2 come from different constructs.** C1 is NFC, which is one thing (enjoyment of thinking). C2 is override tendency, which is a different thing (checking your intuitions). NFC items alone don't measure verification. The CRT paper (Frederick, 2005) confirmed this: you can enjoy thinking without being good at overriding your gut. Our C1/C2 split puts two constructs under one axis. They share a "System 2 engagement" theme (Stanovich & West, 2000) but they're not two halves of one validated scale. We report them separately so any divergence is visible — if pilot data shows them merging, the separate reporting is harmless.
**Axis D facets.**

- **D1 Entry Point:** Riding (1997) Wholist-Analytic. What registers first when you encounter something new — the parts or the whole picture? Riding's original assessment uses reaction-time tasks, not a questionnaire.

- **D2 Decomposition Habit:** Same Riding source, but applied to how you work with information once you have it. Do you break things down, or look for patterns that connect them? D2 is our extension — Riding didn't split Wholist-Analytic into two sub-facets.

**Honesty note 3 — D1 and D2, and the switch from behavioral to self-report.** Riding treats Wholist-Analytic as one dimension and measures it behaviorally (reaction time on computer tasks). We split it into D1 and D2 and use Likert self-report instead. Both moves are design choices. Riding himself warned that self-report has weaknesses for cognitive style ("inability to report accurately… social desirability bias"). We're transparent about this: D1 and D2 are reported separately so you can see any differences; if they turn out to be the same factor, the split is harmless. And the self-report format carries the same limitations every test in this suite has — stated in §10.

**Honesty note 4 — Overlap with personality.** C1 (enjoyment of thinking) overlaps with Big Five Openness-to-Ideas. C2 (verification) overlaps with Conscientiousness. Axis D overlaps weakly with Openness. These are validated constructs — we're not inventing new dimensions, we're combining established ones into a new structure. The MMA's contribution is the combination: two axes that answer "how do you compute?" from different angles (process and structure), framed through Turing's work rather than through personality.
### Facet C1: Deliberation Preference (8 items)
**Never reported as:** an IQ score, a creativity score, a competence ranking, a fixed identity, or a clinical assessment. Always framed as a snapshot of how your mind tends to work right now.

65#TJ:**Honesty note 1 (Axis C compositing).** NFC (rational engagement) and FI (experiential intuition) are orthogonal in the REI (Epstein et al., 1996; r = .08, p < .001 but negligible effect size — "largely independent"). lines: ### 2.5 Facet grounding and honesty notes

The facets under each axis are grounded in validated constructs. Three honesty notes document design choices where we stray from the source instruments — the same transparency Test 1 uses for its Axis A compositing.
**Axis C facets.**

- **C1 Deliberation Preference:** Need for Cognition (Cacioppo & Petty, 1982). The tendency to engage in and enjoy effortful thinking. NFC is one thing — one major factor, confirmed in four studies. Items are about enjoyment: "I prefer complex to simple problems"; "Thinking is not my idea of fun" [reversed]. Not about speed, not about ability.

- **C2 Override Tendency:** The dispositional side of cognitive override (Frederick, 2005). Do you pause and check your intuitions, or trust them and move on? CRT is a behavioral test — our items convert this to self-report, asking about your tendency to verify, not your ability to get the right answer. Stanovich & West (2000) on "cognitive decontextualization" provides the bridge: both C1 and C2 are about engaging System 2, but C1 is about enjoying it and C2 is about checking with it.

**Honesty note 1 — Axis C puts two independent dimensions on one scale.** NFC (enjoyment of rational thinking) and Faith in Intuition (experiential) are separate dimensions in the REI (Epstein et al., 1996; r = .08). A person can be high in both or low in both. Treating them as opposite ends of one axis collapses two dimensions into one. A mid-axis score on our test could mean you're high in both systems, low in both, or genuinely in the middle. The C1 and C2 facet scores help tell these apart: if your C1 (enjoyment) is high but your axis score is mid-range, you're probably bimodal — you engage both rational AND intuitive thinking. The facet signature surfaces this; the axis mean alone doesn't.

**Honesty note 2 — C1 and C2 come from different constructs.** C1 is NFC (enjoyment of thinking). C2 is override tendency (checking your intuitions). These are different things — the CRT paper (Frederick, 2005) confirmed you can enjoy thinking without being good at checking your gut. We put them under one axis because they share a "System 2 engagement" theme (Stanovich & West, 2000), but they're not two halves of one validated scale. We report them separately so any divergence is visible. If pilot data ever shows they merge into one factor, the separate reporting is harmless.
**Axis D facets.**

- **D1 Entry Point:** Riding (1997) Wholist-Analytic. What registers first when you encounter something new — the parts, or the whole picture? Riding's original test uses computer-based reaction-time tasks, not a questionnaire.

- **D2 Decomposition Habit:** Same Riding source, but applied to what you do once you have the information. Do you break things down into units, or look for patterns that connect them? D2 is our extension — Riding doesn't split Wholist-Analytic into two sub-facets.

**Honesty note 3 — D1 and D2, and the switch from behavioral to self-report.** Riding treats Wholist-Analytic as one dimension and measures it behaviorally. We split it into two facets and use Likert self-report. Both are design choices. Riding himself flagged self-report weaknesses for cognitive style ("inability to report accurately… social desirability bias"). We're transparent: D1 and D2 are reported separately so you can see any differences; if they turn out to be the same factor, the split is harmless. The self-report format carries the same caveats as every other test in this suite.

**Honesty note 4 — Overlap with personality.** C1 overlaps with Big Five Openness-to-Ideas. C2 overlaps with Conscientiousness. Axis D overlaps weakly with Openness. These are real, validated constructs — we're not inventing dimensions, we're combining established ones into a new structure. The MMA's contribution is asking "how do you compute?" from two angles (process and structure), framed through Turing's work rather than through personality.

This is the right question. Let me evaluate it against what the papers actually say — not against the framework's lock.

## What the evidence actually says about self-report for cognition

The framework locks Test 2's methodology to Test 1's. But the papers we reviewed disagree with each other on whether that's appropriate:

**The case for self-report (NFC, REI):** Cacioppo & Petty (1982) built and validated the NFC entirely as a self-report Likert scale. Epstein et al. (1996) did the same for the REI. Both instruments work — they predict behavior, discriminate between groups, and show stable factor structures. Self-report *can* measure cognitive dispositions. This is the evidence the framework's lock rests on.

**The case against self-report (Riding, CRT):** Riding (1997) is explicit and sharp about this. He didn't just prefer behavioral assessment — he *rejected* self-report for cognitive style:

> "introspective self-report measures have inherent weaknesses. These include the subject's (i) possible inability to report their behaviour accurately and objectively, (ii) unwillingness to make the necessary effort to respond accurately and (iii) bias due to the pressure of social desirability" (p. 31)

He built the CSA as a reaction-time computer test *because* he believed people cannot accurately self-report how they think. And Frederick's CRT (2005) is behavioral for the same reason — you can't ask someone "do you override your intuitions?" and trust the answer. You have to give them a problem that triggers the wrong intuition and see if they catch it.

The tension is not minor. The two strongest instruments for the constructs we're measuring — Riding's CSA for Encoding Structure and Frederick's CRT for Override Tendency — are both behavioral. The self-report instruments (NFC, REI) exist and work, but they measure a narrower band of the construct space: enjoyment and preference, not actual processing behavior.

## The real difference between Test 1 and Test 2

Test 1 asks "how do you burn?" — about your characteristic energy and social orientation. These are *felt* states. You know whether you wake up charged or groggy. You know whether people energize or drain you. Self-report maps directly onto felt experience.

Test 2 asks "how do you compute?" — about your characteristic cognitive processing. These are often *unconscious* processes. System 1 is automatic by definition. You may not know whether you process parts-first or whole-first — you just do it. The REI's Faith in Intuition scale asks "I trust my gut feelings" — but people with bad intuition also trust their gut. Self-report is a weaker instrument here, and the papers we reviewed confirm this.

This doesn't mean self-report is *invalid* for cognition. It means the measurement error is higher, the ceiling is lower, and the gap between claimed and actual validity is wider than for Test 1. The NFC and REI show it works *well enough* for dispositional constructs. But the strongest behavioral instruments (CSA, CRT) suggest it works *less well* than for affect.

## Three options, evaluated

**Option A: Keep the lock, no changes.** Defend with NFC/REI precedent.

- Pro: Consistent across the suite. Supported by validated instruments.
- Con: Ignores Riding's explicit critique. Implies equal measurement quality to Test 1, which the evidence doesn't support. Less credible.

**Option B: Keep the format, add a Domain-Specific Honesty Note.** Same Likert items, but with a prominent acknowledgment — in the intro and limitations — that self-report is a weaker instrument for cognitive style than for affective disposition, that Riding (1997) specifically rejected it for his own instrument, and that this is an explicit tradeoff for the game context. This is what Test 1 already does for its compositing notes — transparently stating where the framework deviates from the source.

- Pro: Preserves consistency. Strengthens credibility by naming the limitation. Costs nothing. Matches the pattern of honesty notes already in §2.5.
- Con: Doesn't actually improve measurement. Just acknowledges the ceiling.

**Option C: Hybrid — keep the Likert core, add behavioral items.** Keep the 32-item self-report bank but add 2–4 behavioral "challenge" items at the end (optional, clearly separated). These would be CRT-style problems or Riding-style pattern tasks that provide a behavioral signal alongside the self-report. Not scored into the main result — surfaced as a "verification check" or enrichment. This is what a game context uniquely enables: you can add a fun puzzle section that also serves measurement.

- Pro: Genuinely improves measurement. Adds a behavioral signal. Leverages the game format. Directly addresses Riding's and Frederick's critiques.
- Con: Breaks the methodological lock. Requires new item design. The behavioral items would need careful calibration. Adds complexity.

## My recommendation

**Option B is the right call for now.** Here's why:

The lock is not arbitrary — it exists because the suite's credibility depends on equal depth across tests (00 §2: "equal depth, no test accidentally weaker than another"). Breaking the lock for Test 2 would fragment the suite's measurement model and make the synthesis (4 tests → 8-axis profile) harder to interpret.

But the lock doesn't require pretending self-report is equally good for cognition as for affect. The honesty note is the right move: it preserves the method while being transparent about its domain-specific weakness. This is exactly the pattern Test 1 already uses for its compositing notes — "this is what the source says; here's how we deviate; here's why." Test 2 should do the same for its measurement format.

Option C (behavioral enrichment) is genuinely promising and should be explored as a future addition — it's one of the few things a game can offer that a paper questionnaire cannot. But it's a separate scope item and shouldn't hold up the core design.

Let me implement Option B now — a prominent Domain-Specific Honesty Note in §10 (Limitations) and referenced in the honesty statement at the top.

content.thinking:
I'll elevate the Riding critique into its own prominent limitation and also update the honesty statement at the top to reference it. The current line 297 mentions Riding but it's just one sentence in a general bullet. It should be its own paragraph.

Also, I should add a note distinguishing Test 2's measurement challenges from Test 1's: Test 1 measures felt states (easier to self-report); Test 2 measures often-unconscious cognitive processes (harder to self-report). This is the critical distinction the user should understand.

lines: **Limitations, stated up front in the product.**
- Not a validated clinical instrument. Inspired by validated models (NFC, REI, CRT, Wholist-Analytic). Not independently psychometrically evaluated.

- **Domain-specific honesty note — self-report is a weaker instrument for cognitive style than for affect.** Test 1 measures felt states (how energized you feel, how socially oriented you are). Those are accessible to introspection. Test 2 measures cognitive processes (how you process and structure information), which are often unconscious. System 1 is automatic by definition — people may have limited introspective access to their own cognitive style. Riding (1997) built the CSA as a behavioral reaction-time test specifically because he rejected self-report for cognitive style: "introspective self-report measures have inherent weaknesses… inability to report accurately… unwillingness to make the necessary effort… social desirability bias" (p. 31). Frederick's (2005) CRT is likewise behavioral — you cannot ask someone if they override their intuitions and trust the answer; you have to give them a problem and observe. We use self-report Likert because validated instruments exist for this domain (the NFC and REI use it successfully), and a behavioral test is impractical in a self-administered game context. But the measurement error is genuinely higher here than for Test 1, and the ceiling on what self-report can capture for cognitive processing is lower. This is an explicit tradeoff, not an equivalence.

- The REI dimensions (NFC and FI) are orthogonal (Epstein et al., 1996). Collapsing them into one bipolar axis loses information — the facet signature recovers some, not all, of the lost texture. See §2.5 honesty note 1.

edits.lines: > Honesty statement: The MMA is an original, theory-informed assessment for reflection and play. Its two axes are grounded in full-text-verified constructs: Processing Mode draws from Need for Cognition (Cacioppo & Petty, 1982), the Rational-Experiential Inventory (Epstein et al., 1996), and the Cognitive Reflection Test (Frederick, 2005); Encoding Structure draws from Riding's (1997) Wholist-Analytic dimension, with cross-cultural corroboration from Nisbett et al. (2001). It is not independently validated and is not clinical. Self-report Likert is a weaker measurement format for cognitive style than for the affective constructs in Test 1 — cognitive processes are often unconscious, and Riding (1997) and Frederick (2005) both use behavioral assessments for this reason. This is an explicit tradeoff stated in §10. The four result names are an interpretive metaphor drawn from computing and Turing's own work, not a claim that human minds are literally algorithms.

  82#SK:## 3. Why the framework fits the Turing theme
  83#YX:
  84#ZX:Turing's core insight was that there are many valid ways a mind can compute. The Imitation Game asks whether a hidden mind can be inferred from its outputs. The MMA asks the inverse: given your outputs (your item responses), which mode of mind is yours?
  85#SR:
  86#XS:The fit is structural. Turing's own work spans all four quadrants — not as a retrospective mapping, but as a direct correspondence between the cognitive mode each quadrant describes and what Turing actually built or discovered:
  87#XB:
  88#BZ:| Turing's work | Cognitive mode | Why the fit is genuine, not decorative |
  89#PH:|---|---|---|
  90#HV:| The Turing Machine, the Halting Problem (1936) | ⚙️ The Algorithm (sequential + deliberate) | Turing formalized computation as a deterministic sequence of exact operations. The Algorithm is the mode this formalization describes: stepwise, verifiable, each operation justified by the one before it. The Turing Machine IS the operational definition of sequential+deliberate. |
  91#XQ:| Enigma codebreaking, Bombe design (1939–42) | 🕸️ The Cipher (sequential + intuitive) | Cryptanalysis involves sequential operation (character by character, frequency by frequency) driven by pattern recognition rather than formal proof. The Bombe automated this: an electro-mechanical pattern-matcher that tested rotor settings against known cribs. The mapping is to the cognitive mode of the activity, not to Turing's personal style — the weakest of the four mappings, stated openly. |
  92#QY:| Morphogenesis, reaction-diffusion (1952) | 🔮 The Gestalt (holistic + intuitive) | Turing's morphogenesis paper describes how global patterns (spots, stripes, spirals) emerge from simple local rules — the definition of a holistic+intuitive insight. He saw the whole pattern arising from the system dynamics, not from specifying each element. This is the purest expression of the Gestalt mode. |
  93#ZJ:| ACE architecture, computability theory (1945) | 🏗️ The Architecture (holistic + deliberate) | The ACE design was a complete system architecture — Turing designed the whole machine, not a component. His computability work asks what can be computed in principle, a systems-level question approached with formal rigor. The Architecture mode: deliberate, structured, and about wholes. |
  94#MS:
  95#NY:The test's framing: *Turing showed that minds, like machines, come in different architectures. Which of these is yours?* The mapping is structural and historically grounded, not decorative. The one mapping that stretches (the Cipher → Enigma via the mode of the activity, not the man) is stated openly rather than implied.

 137#BP:## 6. Methodology and scoring
 138#KK:
 139#RJ:Inherits Test 1's model identically — the math is construct-agnostic and applies to any two-axis continuous instrument.
 140#XS:
 141#PN:**Step 1, collect.** 32 responses, each 1 to 7. Four facets (C1, C2, D1, D2), 8 items each.
 142#HQ:
 143#QJ:**Step 2, direction-normalize.** Map each item so a higher value always means more Deliberate (Axis C) or more Sequential (Axis D). Reverse-keyed items are inverted.
 144#BT:
 145#ZT:**Step 3, facet scores.** C1 = mean of normalized C1 items, scaled 0–100. Similarly for C2, D1, D2.
 146#JM:
 147#RM:**Step 4, axis scores.** C = mean of C1 and C2, 0–100 (0 = Intuitive, 100 = Deliberate). D = mean of D1 and D2, 0–100 (0 = Holistic, 100 = Sequential).
 148#SS:
 149#MB:**Step 5, locate on the plane.** Center is (50, 50). Quadrant from the signs of C−50 and D−50.
 150#NP:  - C>50, D>50: The Algorithm
 151#SJ:  - C<50, D>50: The Cipher
 152#YM:  - C<50, D<50: The Gestalt
 153#MR:  - C>50, D<50: The Architecture
 154#VY:- Prototypicality r = distance from center / 70.7.
 155#WY:- Gradation convention. Same geometry as Test 1. Within each quadrant, progress is measured from the entry edge (the boundary with the adjacent quadrant). Binned Early (0–30°), Mid (30–60°), Late (60–90°).
 156#RN:**Step 6, classify.** Follows Test 1's v0.19 model.
 157#WY:- **Facet-tension check.** An axis is "tense" when its two facets pull in opposite directions and both are at least 20 points from 50. That means the axis mean landed near center because the two facets cancelled each other — not because you're moderate.
 158#TB:- **r ≥ 0.28** (clear mode): report your mode, gradation, and facet signature. If an axis is tense, add a tension flag.
 159#KH:- **r < 0.28, no tension** (genuinely balanced): report **The Halting Point** — the boundary condition. Named for Turing's proof that no algorithm can determine in general whether a program will halt. Similarly, your responses don't strongly favor any one mode — not a failure, just an honest answer.
 160#KH:- **r < 0.28, with tension** (near center from cancellation): same Halting Point boundary, but the narrative changes. Instead of "you're balanced," it says "you're near center because two strong facets cancel — not because you're moderate. Read the facet signature." This is the tension modifier rewriting the story, not a new result type.
 161#JB:
 162#VH:This is the hybrid dimensional and prototypical pattern (Kerber et al., 2021) inherited from Test 1. It avoids the midpoint cliff (McCrae and Costa, 1989). The Halting Point, like the Threshold in Test 1, is a boundary condition — not a fifth type.

 167#WV:## 7. Question format and response scale
 168#BT:
 169#BQ:Format, response scale, and rationale are identical to Test 1. Summarized here, see `01-solstice-cycle-assessment.md` §7 for the full argument.
 170#KP:The format: each question shows a short scenario and two opposing anchor statements on a seven-point scale. The poles alternate randomly so you can't default to one side. The bipolar format itself handles acquiescence bias (always-agree tendency).
 171#NV:
 172#JV:Every validated cognitive-style instrument uses Likert — the REI, NFC, and CSA are all questionnaire-based. None use sliders. Seven points gives enough precision without overwhelming you.
 173#TT:
 174#SM:---
 175#BN:
 176#WP:**Two lengths, one item bank.** Standard form: 32 questions (~8–10 minutes). Quick form: 16 questions (~4–5 minutes). Both use the same scoring and give the same result types. The 16 is a subset of the 32 — the same items, fewer of them. You can start with 16 and finish the rest later for the full result. The 16-item version is a quick read: it places you in a mode reliably, but the facet detail is rougher (four items per facet lands in a lower reliability band, which we state on the result screen).
 177#HM:
 178#YK:**Facet structure.**
 179#VM:- Axis C, Processing Mode: **C1 Deliberation Preference** (do you enjoy thinking hard?) and **C2 Override Tendency** (do you check your intuitions?). C1 comes from Need for Cognition (Cacioppo & Petty, 1982). But the framework needs two axes total. If we used NFC as Axis 1 and FI as Axis 2, we'd lose Encoding Structure — which is the second genuinely different cognitive dimension. NFC and FI are both about processing mode; Encoding Structure is about something different (how you organize information).

The "intuitive" pole would genuinely be "low deliberate preference" rather than "high experiential." This is actually MORE honest — it doesn't composite two independent dimensions. Let me challenge the core assumption: is the 2-axis bipolar Likert model actually the right instrument for cognitive style? I'll evaluate the alternatives honestly, not preserve the lock by default.

---

## What I reconsidered and what held

### 1. Response format — Likert vs. behavioral

Riding (1997) is explicit: self-report is *weaker* for cognition than for affect. The CSA uses reaction-time tasks. The CRT uses open-ended problems. The best instruments are behavioral.

But the NFC and REI are self-report and they work. The question isn't whether self-report is ideal — it isn't. The question is whether it's *adequate* for a game context where reaction-time measurement and right/wrong scoring are impractical.

Our existing items are actually a hybrid: they're phrased as behavioral scenarios ("You're handed a problem you've never seen before. First move?"), not trait endorsements ("I am a deliberate thinker."). This goes partway toward Riding's philosophy — measuring what you'd *do*, not what you *claim to be* — within a Likert format. The scenario framing reduces but doesn't eliminate the self-report gap.

**Verdict: Keep Likert. It's adequate. The honesty note I added in §10 is the right transparency move. A behavioral enrichment module (optional CRT-style puzzles at the end) is worth exploring later but doesn't replace the core instrument.**

### 2. The bipolar axis vs. using NFC and FI as separate axes

This is the deeper question. Epstein et al. (1996) found NFC and Faith in Intuition are orthogonal (r = .08). They're two independent dimensions. Our current design composites them into one bipolar "Deliberate ↔ Intuitive" axis.

I considered an alternative: use NFC as Axis 1 (enjoyment of thinking, no compositing) and keep Encoding Structure as Axis 2. The "intuitive" pole would genuinely be "low deliberate preference" — no compositing needed, no honesty note required.

This fails for a specific reason: low NFC ≠ intuitive. A person with low NFC simply doesn't enjoy thinking. That could mean they're a rapid, intuitive processor (high FI, low NFC) — or it could mean they're disengaged from thinking entirely (low FI, low NFC). The REI's two dimensions capture this distinction; a single NFC axis collapses it. Someone who is high in both NFC and FI would also score mid-range on a single bipolar axis — the same mid-range ambiguity, just for a different reason.

Our current compositing approach (NFC ↔ FI on one axis) is actually the honest compromise: it acknowledges the problem, uses the two REI dimensions to define both poles, and relies on facet scores (C1 = NFC, the rational contribution) to disambiguate the mid-range. Using NFC alone would trade the documented compositing problem for an undocumented conflation of "intuitive" with "disengaged."

**Verdict: Keep the composited axis. The alternative is worse.**

### 3. The 2-axis 2-facet structure

Riding's Wholist-Analytic is unidimensional. Our D1/D2 split is our own. The NFC is unidimensional; our C1/C2 split is across constructs.

Could we use fewer facets? A simpler model with just 2 axes (no sub-facets) would lose the facet-signature reporting, which is what lets a result say "you're deliberate mostly through enjoyment, not through verification." The facet layer is where the measurement becomes more than a flat quiz. Test 1 established that this is worth the complexity.

Could we use MORE facets? The REI has subscales (NFC, FI, and within FI: intuition, emotionality, imagination). Norris & Epstein (2017) add more experiential subscales. But adding facets increases item count without validated instruments behind them. Two facets per axis is the sustainable floor given the evidence.

**Verdict: Keep the 2-facet structure. It's the right tradeoff between depth and evidence support.**

### 4. Scoring model — the circle/plane geometry

Test 1 has a genuine circumplex (Russell 1980 — affect is circular). Test 2 has a plane (the framework explicitly says only Test 1 is a true circumplex). A plane works for any two continuous dimensions.

The question is whether the 0.28 threshold and the Halting Point boundary condition are appropriate. They are — the midpoint is where neither processing preference nor encoding structure dominates, and the threshold value is designer-set and tunable in both tests. The math is construct-agnostic.

**Verdict: Keep the scoring model. No construct-specific reason to change it.**

### 5. Result types

Algorithm, Cipher, Gestalt, Architecture. These are good. The Turing mappings are verified. The Halting Point boundary condition is a solid parallel to Test 1's Threshold.

I reconsidered the "Halting Point" name. The Halting Problem proves no algorithm can determine in general whether a program halts. A near-center respondent can't be definitively placed in one mode. The metaphor works in one direction: undecidability. But the Halting Problem is about *proof*, not about *uncertainty* — and a boundary respondent isn't formally undecidable, just ambiguous. The metaphor is slightly imprecise.

Alternative names: "The Boundary" (too generic), "The Pause" (too soft), "The Undecidable" (rejected — negative shading). "The Halting Point" is the best of the options considered — it's specific, Turing-referenced, and parallels "The Threshold" as a positional name. I'd keep it.

**Verdict: Keep result types and boundary name.**

---

## The one thing that genuinely should be different: the honesty tier

The measurement gap between Test 1 and Test 2 is real. Test 1 measures felt states — you know whether you're energized or drained, social or solitary. Test 2 measures cognitive processes — you may not know whether you process parts-first, and System 1 operates automatically. The validated behavioral instruments (CSA, CRT) exist precisely because self-report is weaker here.

The right move isn't a methodology change — it's transparently stating that the ceiling is lower. I've added this to both the honesty statement (line 6) and a dedicated paragraph in §10 Limitations. The existing self-report bias note now has teeth: it names Riding's specific rejection of self-report for cognitive style, explains why our context forces the tradeoff, and states that the measurement error is higher than for Test 1. This is the same discipline the compositing honesty notes use — "here's what the source says, here's how we deviate, here's the cost."

---

## Summary: keep the methodology, strengthen the honesty

| Element | Reconsidered? | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Response format | Yes — Riding argues against Likert for cognition | Keep Likert | NFC/REI validate it; our scenario framing partially addresses the critique |
| Bipolar axis compositing | Yes — alternative of using NFC alone is worse | Keep composited axis | NFC alone conflates "intuitive" with "disengaged" |
| 2-axis × 2-facet structure | Yes — sources are unidimensional | Keep structure | Facet reporting adds depth; the DeYoung two-aspect application is transparently disclosed |
| Scoring model | Yes — same as Test 1 | Keep | Math is construct-agnostic; no cognitive-specific reason to change |
| Result types | Yes — names and Turing mappings | Keep | Verified against Turing's actual work; Halting Point is best available name |
| Honesty tier | Yes — measurement gap is real | **Strengthened** | Domain-specific note added to intro + §10; self-report ceiling is explicitly lower here than for Test 1 |
